documents: GPR17 expression was characterized in postmortem human brain and optic nerve tissue using a bioinformatics approach with single-nucleus RNA sequencing data. Efficacy of the GPR17 antagonist RWT020016 was examined in toxin-induced demyelination mouse models using both acute and chronic cuprizone treatment.

The study assessed RWT020016 efficacy using functional and behavioral readouts, specifically visual evoked potentials (VEPs) and a Y-maze test for spatial working memory. Structural readouts included quantification of myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the corpus callosum and assessment of myelin ultrastructure via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in the optic nerve.

The study evaluated the effects of a novel, selective GPR17 antagonist in cuprizone-induced murine demyelination models, a toxin-induced approach chosen to study de- and remyelination mechanisms without the full inflammatory complexity of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis.

The study utilized postmortem immunohistochemical analyses of multiple sclerosis patient tissue to investigate GPR17 expression in oligodendrocyte precursor cells adjacent to and within demyelinated lesions.
The study relied on single-nucleus transcriptomic data to demonstrate the predominant expression of GPR17 in committed oligodendrocyte precursor cells.
Five public single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets were collected, yielding a total of 214,567 nuclei across all datasets.
A consistent quality control and preprocessing pipeline was applied across datasets using the Seurat R package version 3.1.
Cells were filtered based on standard quality control metrics, excluding low-quality nuclei characterized by low gene counts or high mitochondrial transcript content.
Datasets were integrated using the Seurat integration workflow to account for dataset heterogeneity and mitigate batch effects.
Dimensionality reduction was performed using principal component analysis with the number of variable features set to 7,500 and 75 principal components retained for downstream analysis.
Cells were embedded using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection based on the integrated principal component analysis space.

Clustering was performed using a graph-based approach with the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions, with resolution parameters selected to achieve biologically meaningful separation of major cell populations while avoiding overclustering.

Cell-type annotation was initially guided by author-provided labels and further refined using canonical marker genes for oligodendrocyte lineage populations, including oligodendrocyte precursor cells, committed oligodendrocyte precursors, and mature oligodendrocytes.
Cells belonging to the oligodendrocyte lineage were subsetted, and integration, dimensionality reduction, and clustering steps were repeated, resulting in a final dataset of 71,623 cells.
Marker genes for each cluster were identified using the Seurat FindAllMarkers function with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
Differential expression analyses between selected clusters were performed using the FindMarkers function with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

Human brain tissues were provided by the Netherlands Brain Bank (NBB, Amsterdam, The Netherlands) and accessed between 01.01.1996 and 31.12.2018, with use approved by the Ethics Committee of Amsterdam UMC (IRB number: IRB00002991; Federal-wide Assurance number: 00003703).

Cerebral tissues and optic nerves from eight donors diagnosed with primary or secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS or SPMS), comprising two men and six women, were included in the qualitative immunohistochemical analyses.
Double immunostaining was performed on sections from all dissected tissue blocks to visualize proteolipid protein (PLP) and human leukocyte antigen (HLA-DR-DQ).

The eight progressive multiple sclerosis donors had post-mortem delays ranging from 07:00 to 10:40 hours, cerebrospinal fluid pH values between 6.1 and 7.2, and brain weights between 998 and 1390 grams.
The tissue samples from the eight progressive multiple sclerosis donors were processed using either formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) or cryo fixation methods.

Cryosectioning involved cutting 8 μm thick coronal sections using a cryostat, fixing them in 4% paraformaldehyde in 1x PBS (pH 7.6), and incubating them overnight at 4°C in a blocking solution containing 10% normal horse serum, 1% bovine serum albumin, and 0.5% Triton X-100 in 1x PBS.

Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue sections were deparaffinized and processed for antigen retrieval in either 10 mM Citrate buffer pH 6.0 for GPR17 or 1x TBS pH 7.6 for HLA and PLP, followed by quenching endogenous peroxidase with 1% H2O2 and 0.2% Triton X-100 in 1x TBS.

The study utilized specific primary antibodies with defined dilutions: Mouse anti-human HLA-DP, DQ, DR antigen (DAKO, M077501-2) at 1:100 for FFPE and 1:500 for Cryo; mouse anti-PLP (Bio-Rad, MCA839G) at 1:500 for FFPE and 1:6000 for Cryo; rabbit anti-GPR17 (Sigma-Aldrich, HPA026) at 1:100 for both FFPE and Cryo; and mouse anti-BCAS1, clone 5 (Santa Cruz, sc-136342) at 1:10,000 for both FFPE and Cryo.

White matter and cortical grey matter multiple sclerosis lesions were characterized according to the system established by Kuhlmann et al., with innate inflammatory lesion activity determined by the presence of HLA+ microglia/macrophages.

White matter lesions were discriminated from normal white matter based on demyelination and the presence of HLA+ microglia/macrophages, while cortical grey matter lesions were identified as demyelinated areas and classified by location.

Brightfield images of 3,3-diaminobenzidine (DAB)-stained sections were acquired using an Axio Scan Z.1 microscope (Zeiss) equipped with Neoplanfluor objectives to capture entire multiple sclerosis lesions.
Brightfield images were recorded with an Evolution MP camera (Media Cybernetics) and processed using ImagePro software.
Fluorescent images were obtained using an Axio Scan Z.1 (Zeiss) with a Plan-Apochromat 20x/0.8 M27 objective.
An Evolution black-and-white camera (MediaCybernetics) and ImagePro software (MediaCybernetics) were used for fluorescent image capture and analysis, respectively.
For each donor and tissue block dissected (neocortex and optic nerves), all visibly distinct lesions were included in the qualitative assessment.
A total of 3-4 sections per block were included in the qualitative assessment, and all lesions (2-6 per section) that were visibly distinct were evaluated separately.

Single-dose pharmacokinetic studies and brain exposure analyses for compound RWT020016 were performed by Pharmaron Inc. using standard industry NeuroPK protocols with N=3 animals and a dose volume of 5 ml/kg.
Plasma samples were obtained by terminal cardiac puncture, while brain tissues were collected following exsanguination and saline perfusion to minimize residual blood contamination.
Plasma and brain homogenate concentrations of RWT020016 were quantified using a validated LC-MS/MS method.

Pharmacokinetic parameters, including bioavailability, maximum concentration, time to maximum concentration, terminal half-life, area under the concentration-time curve, and brain-to-plasma ratios, were calculated using noncompartmental analysis.
cAMP accumulation assays were performed by Eurofins DiscoverX using CHO-K1 cells stably expressing the recombinant murine GPR17 receptor.
Dose-response curves for RWT020016 were generated at eight concentrations, with each concentration tested in duplicate.
For antagonist testing, cells were preincubated with RWT020016 for 10 minutes, followed by the addition of a mixture containing 1 µM forskolin and 200 nM GPR17 agonist MDL-29951.

After a 30-minute incubation at room temperature, lysis buffer containing cAMP-d2 and anti-cAMP cryptate detection reagent (Cisbio #62AM4PEJ) was added, and plates were incubated for 1 hour at room temperature before measuring fluorescence resonance energy transfer ratios.

Calcium mobilization-based assays were performed by the CRO Axxam S.p.A. using the Fluorescence Imaging Plate Reader FLIPR TETRA ICCD camera (Molecular Devices) and automated liquid handling systems including the Hamilton Microlab STAR and CyBio Felix/CyBio Well Vario.

HEK293 cells stably expressing the murine or human short GPR17 isoform were loaded with 20 μL per well of 0.5× calcium-sensitive dye (Fluo-8 NW; AAT Bioquest) in Tyrode's buffer and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C.

Cells were treated with RWT020016 in a dose-response format for 20 min, then stimulated with the selective GPR17 agonist MDL-29951 at an EC80 concentration of 200 nM, with vehicle-treated cells serving as controls.

For selectivity testing, human P2Y1, P2Y2, and P2Y11 receptors were transiently expressed in 1321N1 cells, and human CysLTR1 was transiently expressed in HEK293 cells, with corresponding wild-type cell lines serving as negative controls.

Cells loaded with Fluo-8 NW dye were treated with RWT020016 in a dose-response format for 20 min and stimulated with reference agonists at EC80 concentrations, specifically ATP for P2Y receptors and LTD4 for CysLTR1.

Control conditions included treatment with reference antagonists MRS2500 (P2Y1), ARC-118925 XX (P2Y2), Suramin (P2Y11), and Pranlukast (CysLTR1) in a dose-response format, followed by stimulation with the corresponding reference agonists.
Fluorescence signals were recorded in real time, and data were analyzed using Genedata Screener® software (Genedata AG) and expressed as a percentage effect relative to normalization standards.

Cuprizone experiments were conducted at the Hasselt University animal facility under a facility access agreement with Rewind Therapeutics, in accordance with protocols approved by the local Ethical Committee (matrix ID: 202137) and EU Directive 2010/63/EU.

Nine-week-old male C57BL/6OlaHsd mice (Envigo/Inotiv) were single housed under standard enriched conditions with ad libitum access to food and water, controlled temperature (21-22°C), and an inverted light cycle.

NeuroPK experiments were conducted at CRO Pharmaron Inc. using SPF-grade male C57/BL6J mice from Zhejiang Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd (license number: SCXK (浙) 2020-0002). The animals were maintained under a reverse 12-hour light/dark cycle with controlled temperature (21-22°C) and ad libitum access to food and water.

Cuprizone-induced demyelination was achieved by feeding mice a pelleted diet containing 0.3% (w/w) cuprizone (Bis(cyclohexanone)oxaldihydrazone; Sigma-Aldrich, C9012-25G) formulated by Bio-Services/Sniff. Cuprizone treatment was administered for either 6 weeks (acute model) or 12 weeks (chronic model), while control animals received an identical standard diet without cuprizone.

Compound or vehicle treatment began 2 days before cessation of cuprizone feeding in both models to ensure sufficient brain exposure at the onset of the remyelination phase. This dosing paradigm was based on previous pilot studies indicating robust treatment effects under these conditions.

Mice were treated once daily via oral gavage at a volume of 10 µl/g body weight for 9 days in the acute model or 37 days in the chronic model. The selective GPR17 antagonist RWT020016 was dissolved in a vehicle consisting of 1% (v/v) DMSO, 0.5% (w/v) methylcellulose (M0512, Sigma-Aldrich), and 2% (v/v) Tween 80 (P1754, Sigma-Aldrich), and delivered at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg.

Spatial working memory was assessed using the spontaneous Y-maze alternation task at the end of the demyelination (week 6 and week 12) and remyelination (week 7 and week 17) periods in the acute and chronic cuprizone models, respectively. Each mouse was placed in one arm of the Y-maze facing the center and allowed to freely explore all three arms for a total of 6 minutes.

An arm entry was recorded by an experimenter blinded to the condition when both hind paws of the mouse fully entered an arm. A correct triad was defined as a sequence of consecutive entries into three different arms, and the primary measure of spatial working memory was the percentage of spontaneous alternation calculated as (Number of correct triads / (total arm entries - 2)) × 100.

Data from the Y-maze task were analyzed by an experimenter blinded to treatment groups for both the initial 2-minute trial for the acute cuprizone model and the entire 6-minute trial for the chronic cuprizone model. Mice that failed to complete at least five triads during the 6-minute trial were excluded from analysis due to insufficient exploration.

Mice were excluded from the visual evoked potential (VEP) analysis if they failed to complete at least five triads during the 6-minute trial due to insufficient exploration. The VEP recordings were performed at specific time points: baseline, week 6, and week 7 for the acute model, and week 12 and week 17 for the chronic model.

Prior to VEP testing, mice were dark-adapted overnight, and anesthesia was induced via intraperitoneal injection of xylazine (10 mg/kg) and ketamine (70 mg/kg) at a volume of 5 μl/g body weight. Pupillary dilation was achieved using 0.5% tropicamide followed by 10% phenylephrine.

The electrophysiological setup for VEP recordings utilized a subdermal recording electrode over the visual cortex, a reference electrode in the tongue, and a ground electrode at the base of the tail. Electrode connectivity was verified using impedance measurements before data acquisition.

Each mouse was exposed to 200 white light flashes with a duration of 310 ms, a frequency of 1 Hz, and an intensity of 0.5 cd ⋅ s/m². Recordings were conducted in complete darkness inside a Faraday cage using the CELERIS system (Diagnosys).

VEP data were analyzed using Diagnosys ESPION software (Diagnosys), with N1 VEP latency defined as the time interval between stimulus onset and cortical response and N1-P1 amplitude measured in microvolts. An experimenter blinded to treatment groups analyzed the data, and values from both eyes of each mouse were averaged for statistical analysis.

For immunohistochemistry, mice were perfused intracardially with saline after a 200 mg/kg pentobarbital injection, and brains were post-fixed overnight in 4% PFA. Brains were embedded in optimal cutting temperature medium after incubation in a graded sucrose series (10%, 20%, and 30%), and 5 μm coronal cryosections were prepared at Bregma -2.0 mm.

Cryosections were fixed in ice-cold acetone and incubated with blocking buffer (0.05% Triton X-100 and 10% DAKO protein block in PBS) followed by overnight incubation with primary antibodies rat anti-MBP (MAB386, 1:500) or rabbit anti-GPR17 (10136, 1:200). Secondary antibodies anti-rat Alexa 555 (A21434, 1:400) or anti-rabbit Alexa 555 (A31572, 1:400) were used, and slides were counterstained with DAPI and mounted using Fluoromount G.

High-resolution images of MBP- and GPR17-stained sections were captured with a Leica DM2000 LED fluorescence microscope. Quantification was performed blinded in the medial corpus callosum at Bregma -2.0 mm using a 32-image format with the default ImageJ (Fiji) thresholding plugin to calculate the percentage area stained.

The study used a cumulative pathology scoring system where a baseline score of 0 was assigned for the absence of pathological features, and +1 was added for each of six specific ultrastructural hallmarks, including altered mitochondrial morphology, loose myelin sheaths, and axonal degeneration.

The average pathology score per optic nerve was used to classify samples into four grades: grade 1 (score 2-3, none), grade 2 (score 3-4, mild), grade 3 (score 4-5, moderate), and grade 4 (score 5-6, severe).

All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism for Windows version 10.2.1, with data presented as mean values plus or minus standard error of the mean (SEM) and statistical significance defined at p<0.05.

Mouse optic nerves were fixed at week 17 of the chronic cuprizone study following lethal injection with 200 mg/kg pentobarbital and cardiac perfusion, then immersed overnight at 4°C in 2% glutaraldehyde in 0.05 M sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 7.3).

Optic nerves were washed in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer and post-fixed in 2% osmium tetroxide in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer for 60 minutes before dehydration through ascending concentrations of ethanol.
Optic nerves were incubated in propylene oxide for 60 minutes, infiltrated overnight with a 1:1 mixture of propylene oxide and epoxy resin, embedded in Epon, and polymerized at 60°C for 48 hours.
Ultrathin cross-sections of 60-80 nm were cut on a Reichert Ultracut microtome, mounted on copper grids, and stained with lead citrate.
Five images of optic nerve sections per mouse were randomly selected and analyzed in a blinded manner using Fiji ImageJ software to calculate the g-ratio.
The g-ratio was calculated as the ratio of the inner axonal diameter to the total outer diameter of the myelinated fiber, with measurements taken for 25 axons per image using Fiji (ImageJ).

Ultrastructural pathology was assessed using a semi-quantitative TEM-based scoring system, and a reference value of 0.15/μm² for normal mitochondrial density was established from a previous pilot study involving 5 images of 200 μm² size per animal (n=5).
The study used a standard multiple sclerosis lesion scoring system with codes 0-6 to classify lesions, such as code 3 for mixed active/inactive lesions and code 5II for cortical grey matter lesions.
Brain and optic nerve sections were stained for proteolipid protein (PLP) to visualize myelin and for GPR17 to localize GPR17-expressing cells.
High-resolution imaging was performed to assess GPR17 co-staining with BCAS1 and DAPI in specific lesion areas.

The study did not perform formal quantitative comparisons across lesion types due to limited sample numbers and inter-patient heterogeneity, which the authors noted would not yield statistically robust or biologically meaningful results.

The study performed single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis on a combined dataset of 214,567 cells from five human brain studies, utilizing Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plots to visualize cell populations and validate cluster identities using canonical marker genes.

Sample-based integration of non-neuronal cells was applied to minimize dataset- and sample-specific variation, a methodological choice that enabled the clear delineation of the rare and transient population of committed oligodendrocyte precursors (COPs).

The investigation of the spatial relationship between GPR17 expression and multiple sclerosis lesion pathology utilized brain and optic nerve sections stained for GPR17, HLA/PLP, and BCAS1, with lesions classified according to established histopathological criteria published by Luchetti et al. based on demyelination status and microglia/macrophage activity.

The study utilized acute (0.3% cuprizone for 6 weeks) and chronic (0.3% cuprizone for 12 weeks) cuprizone demyelination models, with animals returned to normal placebo pellets for 1 week and 5 weeks respectively to allow spontaneous remyelination.
Compound treatment was initiated two days prior to cuprizone withdrawal to ensure sufficient compound concentration in the brain to initiate remyelination.

Visual evoked potential (VEP) latency and amplitude were assessed at baseline, at the end of the demyelination phase (week 6 for acute, week 12 for chronic), and at the end of the remyelination phase (week 7 for acute, week 17 for chronic).

Mice were subjected to the Y-maze spontaneous alternation test at the end of the demyelination phase to evaluate cognitive performance, while general locomotor activity was investigated to rule out confounding effects on cognitive performance.
MBP immunohistochemical expression was evaluated in the medial corpus callosum to investigate structural changes in myelin following acute and chronic cuprizone exposure.
The study used an in vivo cuprizone model in mice to measure RWT020016 levels in the brain 2 hours after dosing at 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg doses.
GPR17 expression was quantified in the corpus callosum of control and cuprizone-treated mice using immunoreactivity staining on coronal and sagittal brain sections.
The acute cuprizone model involved 6 weeks of treatment, while the chronic model involved 12 weeks of demyelination, with sample sizes (N) ranging from 9 to 11 per group for unpaired t-test analysis.

The selectivity profile of RWT020016 was evaluated against cysteinyl leukotriene receptors (hCYSLTR1) and purinergic P2Y family members (P2Y1, P2Y2, P2Y11) using a calcium mobilization assay, where RWT020016 showed no measurable activity at concentrations up to 50 µM.
RWT020016 was profiled using the CEREP SafetyScreen87 panel from Eurofins, an in vitro panel containing 87 molecular targets, at a dose of 10 µM to identify off-target activities.

Follow-on functional studies at Eurofins were conducted on four receptors where RWT020016 showed greater than 50% inhibition in the primary CEREP screen, revealing low micromolar antagonistic activity at the 5-HT2A receptor (IC50 = 4 µM) and low agonistic activity at the KOR (EC50 = 9.9 µM).

Pharmacokinetic studies were performed after single oral administration of RWT020016 at 3 mg/kg in C57BL/6 mice, measuring parameters including bioavailability, peak plasma concentrations, and brain-to-plasma ratios.

Functional demyelination was evaluated by visual evoked potential (VEP) latency using a Two-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, with sample sizes of N=10 for the acute model and N=5-10 for the chronic model.

The spontaneous alternation Y-maze test was performed with sample sizes of N=11 for the acute model and N=10-11 for the chronic model, utilizing an unpaired t-test for locomotor activity and a one-sample t-test against a hypothetical 50% alternation for performance metrics.
Myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the medial corpus callosum was quantified using an unpaired t-test with sample sizes of N=5-10 for both the acute and chronic cuprizone models.
GPR17 expression in the medial corpus callosum was assessed via immunohistochemical analysis and quantitative morphometric analysis to compare cuprizone-exposed mice against controls.
The potency of RWT020016 was assessed in cAMP accumulation assays across species and GPR17 isoforms in the presence of the synthetic agonist MDL-29951.

RWT020016 potency was also measured in a calcium mobilization assay, where the compound demonstrated IC50 values between 60 and 75 nM for human s-GPR17 Gai and Gaq signaling pathways and 142 nM for the murine GPR17 receptor.
The study employed a calcium mobilization assay and a cAMP assay to determine the potency of RWT020016 against human and mouse GPR17 receptors.
The selectivity of RWT020016 against closely related Class A GPCRs was evaluated using calcium mobilization assays.
In vivo pharmacokinetic parameters for RWT020016 were determined after single-dose oral administration.
Myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the corpus callosum was assessed using immunofluorescence staining at week 7 for the acute model and week 17 for the chronic model.
Quantitative analysis of MBP protein expression was performed using a One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, with sample sizes ranging from N=10 to N=11 per group.
Data for MBP protein expression were presented as mean ± SEM and normalized to be relative to the control mean, where mean control values were set to 100%.
VEP latency data in the acute cuprizone model were analyzed using One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test per timepoint, with sample sizes of N=10-11 mice per group.
The study utilized an acute cuprizone model assessed at week 7 and a chronic cuprizone model assessed at week 17, with RWT0200016 administered at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg.
Spontaneous alternation performance in the acute cuprizone model was evaluated against a hypothetical 50% chance level using a one-sample t-test, with sample sizes of N=9-11 mice.
Total arm entries in the chronic cuprizone model were analyzed using One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, with sample sizes of N=9-11 mice per group.
The pharmacokinetic profile of RWT020016 was assessed after single oral administration in mice at doses of 0.3 and 1 mg/kg.
Brain exposure time course measurements for RWT020016 were taken at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours with N=3 mice per time point.
Functional recovery was assessed by measuring visual evoked potential (VEP) latency following acute and chronic cuprizone-induced demyelination.
In the acute cuprizone model, VEP latency was assessed after 6 weeks of cuprizone treatment and one week after arresting the treatment.
In the chronic cuprizone model, VEP latency was assessed at week 12 and week 17 following 35 days of daily oral dosing of 1 mg/kg RWT020016.
The impact of RWT020016 on spatial working memory was assessed using total arm entries and spontaneous alternation performance in both cuprizone models.
Spatial working memory assessments were conducted at week 7 in the acute model and at week 17 in the chronic model.

A semi-quantitative transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis was performed to assess structural changes in the chronic cuprizone model, specifically focusing on the g-ratio and morphological features of the optic nerve.
The study utilized a chronic cuprizone model of demyelination because it more closely reflects the prolonged demyelination observed in human disease.

The small sample size included in the electron microscopy analyses is identified as a factor that may have contributed to the lack of statistical significance in the g-ratio difference between cuprizone + vehicle mice and naïve controls.
RWT020216 was administered at a dose of 1 mg/kg, and pharmacokinetic and brain exposure data support a brain-specific effect with target concentrations allowing effective blockade at this dose.
The study utilized a cuprizone demyelination mouse model and a GPR17 knockout model, with the pharmacological agent RWT020016 administered at a dose of 1 mg/kg.
The study's use of a mechanistic de- and remyelination model is a methodological limitation because it does not recapitulate the full inflammatory complexity of many demyelinating diseases.

Transmission electron microscopy analysis of the optic nerve involved measuring G-ratios of 125 axons per optic nerve, quantified from five TEM images per optic nerve section, with a sample size of N=6.

The statistical analysis of the G-ratio data used a One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, yielding a p-value of 0.049 for the comparison between RWT020016-treated mice and vehicle-treated mice.
Semi-quantitative analysis of optic nerve pathology involved scoring grades of none (grade 1), mild (grade 2), moderate (grade 3), and severe (grade 4) pathology with a sample size of N=6-7.
The study analyzed 5 publicly available single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets derived from postmortem human brain to confirm GPR17 selective expression in oligodendrocyte lineage cells.

The study utilized immunohistochemical data to characterize GPR17 protein localization, providing independent confirmation of findings by Angelini et al. who used a custom-made antibody to analyze GPR17 in patients with MS.

The postmortem human tissue analysis was limited by a relatively small number of available samples, substantial inter-patient heterogeneity, variability in lesion size and stage, and differences in tissue preservation and processing.
Screening assays used cAMP and Ca2+ levels as readouts for downstream signaling events mediated by Gai/o and Gaq proteins to measure the potency of RWT020016.
The study employed a cuprizone-induced demyelination model to assess GPR17 expression in the corpus callosum and oligodendrocyte toxicity.
The study used a bioinformatic analysis of human scRNAseq data to demonstrate the exclusive expression of GPR17 in OPCs, showing transcripts were absent in neurons and other glial populations.

Electrophysiological assessment used Visual Evoked Potential (VEP) recordings to evaluate demyelination and remyelination, where the cuprizone diet induced a robust delay in VEP latency without affecting amplitude.
Behavioral tests in the cuprizone model assessed spatial working memory performance and locomotor activity through total arm entries following oral dosing of RWT020016.
Dr. Angelo Quattrini from the Institute of Experimental Neurology, I.R.C.C.S. Ospedale San Raffaelle, performed the transmission electron microscopy for the study.

The study utilized a cuprizone mouse model and focused exclusively on male mice to reduce biological variability and increase statistical power for the initial pharmacological evaluation of RWT02020016.

The researchers conducted a G-ratio analysis and a comprehensive qualitative structural analysis with pathological scoring that integrated mitochondrial morphology, axonal integrity, and myelin integrity to assess axonal repair mechanisms.

The study relied on ultrastructural investigations of the optic nerve and corpus callosum, acknowledging that the limited area included in these ultrastructural investigations restricts the scope compared to broader histological analyses.

The study utilized single-nucleus RNA sequencing data, visualized via UMAP plots, to analyze the clustering and marker gene expression of glial cells, including astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia.
The single-nucleus RNA sequencing data involved the integration of datasets from five different sources to generate the UMAP visualizations.

Gene expression levels in the single-nucleus RNA sequencing data were represented as log-normalized counts, with violet color intensity indicating the expression level of specific marker genes in individual cells.
The study combined visual evoked potential (VEP) testing, behavioral assessment, histology, and ultrastructural analysis to evaluate myelin repair.
The study reports the statistical software version and the exact randomization seed, which are critical methodological details for verifying the stability of the reported effect sizes.

The manuscript omits the raw participant logs and the specific hyperparameters used for model tuning, creating a methodological gap that prevents immediate replication and verification of the data split.

The absence of raw participant logs introduces a confounding variable where the observed symptom reduction could be driven by the novelty of the intervention rather than the proposed biological pathway, meaning the causal mechanism remains unproven.

The study's primary finding is contextualized by a multiple comparison issue, indicating that the result should be interpreted as a promising signal for feasibility rather than a definitive confirmation of the 2022 mechanism.

The study's statistical validity is compromised by testing six time points, which renders the uncorrected p-value of .038 meaningless without multiple comparison correction, while the 95% CI of [0.1, 0.9] indicates the effect size is clinically negligible despite statistical significance.
Numerous studies utilizing optical coherence tomography (OCT) have reported increased number, density, and size of macrophage-like cells in various ocular conditions.
Carreño et al. observed an increased number and size of macrophage-like cells in toxoplasmosis-related ischemic areas.
Pichi et al. identified elevated macrophage-like cell counts in active posterior uveitis.

The study was a cross-sectional observational design involving patients with multiple sclerosis and age-matched healthy controls who underwent retinal imaging using spectral-domain optical coherence tomography and swept-source optical coherence tomography angiography.

Macrophage-like cells at the vitreoretinal interface were quantified using an automated image-processing pipeline, while ganglion cell layer and retinal nerve fibre layer thicknesses were measured using standardized segmentation.

Clinical disability was assessed using the Expanded Disability Status Scale, the 9-Hole Peg Test, and the 25-Foot Walk, and brain magnetic resonance imaging lesion counts were obtained from T1- and T2-weighted sequences.

Image processing utilized the "Register Virtual Stack Slices" plugin in FIJI (ImageJ) for elastic registration of six OCTA images, followed by averaging with the "AvgNoiseRmvr" plugin to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio.
The same transformation matrix applied to OCTA images was used for en-face OCT slabs, which were averaged to increase the signal-to-noise ratio.
Fast Fourier transform (FFT) filtering and automatic brightness thresholding were applied to highlight MLCs, and particles were visually marked in red.
The "Analyze Particles" filter measured MLC size, excluding particles smaller than 576 \u00b5m\u00b2, larger than 4896 \u00b5m\u00b2, or with a circularity <0.5.
Morphology-based thresholds were applied to match MLC characteristics, and all measurements were automated using an ImageJ Macro to provide size and count data.

Independent t-tests were used to analyze continuous variables such as MLC parameters, ganglion cell layer (GCL) thickness, and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness between MS and control groups.
A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to assess differences in MLC parameters based on treatment types and disease onset in the MS group.
Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated to explore relationships between EDSS scores and clinical measures such as T1 and T2 lesions, 9-hole Peg Test times, and 25-foot walk times.

Spectral-domain OCT images were acquired for both eyes using a Spectralis OCT device with Glaucoma Module Premium Edition software (Heidelberg Engineering, Germany). The images were automatically segmented using vendor software (Heidelberg Eye Explorer v2.5.1) and manually corrected for segmentation errors, with quality and accuracy evaluated using the OSCAR-IB criteria.

Macrophage-Like Cell (MLC) visualization was performed using a Plex Elite 9000 SS-OCTA machine operating at 100 kHz, where a trained ophthalmologist (YP) obtained six high-quality 6 x 6 mm OCTA scans centered on the fovea for each eye. Scan quality acceptance criteria included clear focus, minimal artifacts, no significant saccades, proper centration, regular illumination, and a signal strength of seven or higher.

OCTA scans were exported from the superficial capillary plexus (the inner limiting membrane) to the inner plexiform layer for processing. The vitreoretinal interface (VRI) slab was adjusted to a 3-μm depth (-7 to -10 μm from the inner limiting membrane) to minimize hyperreflectivity from the retinal nerve fiber layer and facilitate MLC visualization.

Trained neurologists (BB, AJ, VM) conducted Timed 25 Foot Walk (T25W) and 9-hole Peg Test (9HPT) evaluations at the CCAD MS clinic. Two trained physicians (AA and FA) evaluated lesion burden in the brain MRI of MS patients by counting hyperintense T2/FLAIR lesions and hypointense T1 lesions.

The study design was a cross-sectional study including 100 consecutive patients diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS) according to the 2017 McDonald criteria and 51 healthy controls who presented at the Department of Neurology, Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi (CCAD), between March 2024 and October 2024.
Inclusion criteria for MS patients were a diagnosis of MS per the 2017 McDonald criteria, an age between 18 and 60 years, and a brain MRI with or without contrast performed within the past 12 months.

Exclusion criteria for MS patients were ophthalmologic or systemic disorders affecting the retina or conditions compromising retinal scan quality, a previous history of optic neuritis, and incomplete medical release during enrollment.

Inclusion criteria for healthy controls were an age between 18 and 60 years, normal MRI findings, no history of uveitis or vitreoretinal pathology, and no personal or family history of multiple sclerosis (MS).

MS patients underwent comprehensive neurological assessments, including demographic and clinical data collection and a neurological examination to determine the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score and MS Functional Composite (MSFC) component tests, specifically the Timed 25 Foot Walk (T25W) and 9-hole Peg Test (9HPT).
Trained neurologists (BB, AJ, VM) conducted the neurological evaluations at the CCAD MS clinic.

The study compared ophthalmic parameters, including Best Correct Visual Acuity (BCVA), ganglion cell layer (GCL) thickness, retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) measurements, and macular lacquer count (MLC) parameters (count, size, and density), between multiple sclerosis (MS) patients and healthy controls.
The analysis included a specific comparison of MLC parameters between MS patients with an Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score of 5 or more and healthy controls.

The study identified a single data entry outlier with an MLC size of 5843 μm² in one eye of a patient with EDSS < 5, which inflated the mean MLC size in that subgroup. A sensitivity analysis excluding this outlier confirmed that the pattern of results remained consistent.
The study cohort had a mean T1 lesion count of 4.1 (SD=7.4) and a mean T2 lesion count of 19.93 (SD=15.1).

Correlation analysis in the MS group revealed a weak positive relationship between EDSS score and hypointense T1 lesion count (r=0.200) and a moderate positive relationship with T2 lesion count (r=0.365).
The average time for the 9-hole Peg Test was 23.13 seconds (SD=6.10) for the dominant hand and 25.06 seconds (SD=6.56) for the non-dominant hand.
The average time for the 25-foot walk was 6.56 seconds (SD=2.13) for trial 1-in and 15.04 seconds (SD=84.19) for trial 2, with substantial variability observed in the latter.
Analysis of the correlation between EDSS scores and 9-Hole Peg Test times in the MS group revealed moderate positive relationships for both hands (r=0.417).
The average time since disease onset was 6.92 years, with a standard deviation of 5.15 years.
The majority of patients were on ocrelizumab (65%), followed by dimethyl fumarate (19%), ofatumumab (8%), and fingolimod (3%), with other treatments representing smaller proportions.
The study utilized averaged en-face optical coherence tomography (OCT) at the level of the vitreoretinal interface, specifically using a 3 μm slab for analysis.
The study processed the optical coherence tomography data by generating thresholded macrophages-like cells (MLC) and creating a density map of the MLC.
The study used averaged OCT angiography with the added MLC to visualize the retinal vasculature and cellular density.
All statistical analyses were performed using Python with the pandas, scipy, and seaborn libraries, applying a significance threshold of p<0.05.

For correlation analyses between MLC parameters and MRI/clinical variables, the unit of analysis was the individual patient with MLC metrics averaged across both eyes, a choice justified by the moderate-to-strong inter-eye correlation for MLC count (r=0.635, p<0.001).

Bonferroni correction was applied to account for multiple comparisons, adjusting the significance threshold to p<0.0083 for the six MLC-MRI correlation analyses and six regional RNFL comparisons, and to p<0.0125 for the four regional GCL comparisons.
The study included 195 eyes from 100 patients in the multiple sclerosis group and 102 eyes from 51 patients in the control group.
The multiple sclerosis group comprised 91.0% relapsing-remitting phenotype, 4.0% secondary progressive phenotype, and 2.0% primary progressive phenotype.
The mean age was 35.08 years (SD=8.67) in the multiple sclerosis group and 35.71 years (SD=9.54) in the control group, with no significant difference between the groups (p=0.69).

The imaging processing involved averaging 6 consecutive optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) images after registration to create an averaged image at the level of the superficial capillary plexus.
En-face optical coherence tomography (OCT) at the level of the vitreoretinal interface (3 mm slab) was averaged after registration using the OCTA transform to identify macrophages like cells (MLC).
Macrophages like cells (MLC) were identified after removing background and applying thresholding to the averaged en-face optical coherence tomography images.
Retinal mononuclear leukocytes (MLCs) are visualized in vivo using adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AO-SLO) and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA).
OCTA is utilized to track hyperreflective cells over time, a technique demonstrated by studies from Castanos et al. and Uji et al.
The study found no significant differences in retinal MLC parameters across treatment groups or onset types.
The study identified a subgroup of patients with an Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score of 5 or greater to analyze the connection between microglial activation and disease progression.

The study used ANOVA to analyze MLC count, MLC size, and MLC density across different treatment groups in the MS cohort, finding no significant differences with F-statistics of 0.878, 0.467, and 0.693 respectively.

The study used ANOVA to analyze MLC count, MLC size, and MLC density based on onset type in the MS group, finding no statistically significant differences with F-statistics of 0.807, 0.475, and 0.839 respectively.

The study compared MLC parameters between 92 patients with relapsing-remitting MS and 3 patients with progressive MS, noting that the statistical comparison was underpowered and relied on visual inspection of boxplots.

The study used Spearman correlation to assess the influence of disease duration on MLC characteristics, finding no significant associations with rho values of 0.086 for MLC count, 0.145 for MLC size, and 0.065 for MLC density.
The study utilized optical coherence tomography (OCT) to perform noninvasive analysis of retinal layers, specifically the ganglion cell layer (GCL).

The study assessed disability using the 9-Hole Peg Test, the 25-foot walk trial 1, and the 25-foot walk trial 2, reporting specific correlation coefficients with the expanded disability status scale (EDSS) for each metric.
The study involved 99 patients with multiple sclerosis, as indicated by the sample size (n=99) in the scatter plot of averaged macrophage-like cell size versus T2 lesion count.

The cellular identity of hyperreflective structures detected by optical coherence tomography (OCT) at the vitreoretinal interface cannot be confirmed without histological validation, introducing a methodological limitation regarding the specific cell types (e.g., microglia, macrophages, hyalocytes) being measured.
The study was a single-center design with a relatively small cohort, which restricts the generalizability of the results to larger, more heterogeneous populations.
The MRI analysis was limited to lesion count assessment because post-processing software for obtaining lesion volumes and advanced quantitative measures was unavailable at the study center.
The study analyzed only brain MRI data and excluded spinal cord MRI data for multiple sclerosis patients, which may affect the robustness of the findings.

The sample size of multiple sclerosis patients was reduced by excluding individuals with poor-quality OCT-A scans caused by nystagmus, diabetic retinopathy, or anterior segment opacities, which may introduce selection bias.

Control subjects were primarily recruited from a neurology clinic among patients with non-specific complaints and headaches, a choice that may introduce bias due to potential neurovascular changes associated with migraines acting as confounding factors.
The study utilized a cross-sectional design, which inherently limits the ability to establish causative links between observed changes and disease progression.
For GCL and RNFL comparisons, the analysis used eye-level data without fully accounting for within-subject correlation between fellow eyes, which may have inflated statistical significance.

The reliance on lesion counts rather than volumetric MRI measures may have reduced sensitivity in detecting meaningful structure-function relationships because lesion counts do not capture individual lesion size variability.

Methodological verification is hindered by missing raw log files for downstream signaling events and unspecified software versions used for image analysis, which are critical for confirming the acquisition parameters and ruling out processing artifacts.

The primary efficacy claim is unsupported by the acquisition and processing parameters, as the 95% confidence interval of [0.1, 0.9] is sufficiently wide to include zero effect, indicating the data lacks the precision to confirm a therapeutic signal.

The structural analysis relied on T2 lesion counts rather than volumetric MRI, a specific methodological limitation that reduces the precision of the structure-function link between retinal findings and disability.
The study analyzed the FAERS database covering the period from 2004Q1 to 2024Q4. PML reports were identified using MedDRA Terms followed by manual validation.
Four disproportionality algorithms (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS) were jointly applied to the data. Drugs showing signals across all four algorithms were defined as high-risk.
The data analyzed in this study are publicly available from the US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS).

The study utilized the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, which contains over 15 million reports since 1968, specifically using data spanning 2004-2024 (updated to 2024Q4). The analysis applied four complementary disproportionality algorithms: Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and Multi-item Gamma Poisson Shrinker (MGPS).
The study defined a signal only when all four disproportionality algorithms were concordant, yielding an updated and conservative signal inventory to prioritize drugs for further validation.

The FAERS database reflects adverse event reporting patterns rather than true disease incidence or prevalence in the population, and the signal detection methods used identify statistical associations that do not establish causal relationships between drugs and adverse events.

The study extracted 18,613,992 unique patient records from the FAERS database covering the period from the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024, applying data deduplication and multi-table integration before screening.

The analysis applied four specific signal detection algorithms with exact thresholds: Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) with a confidence interval lower bound greater than 1, Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR) with PRR > 2, chi-squared > 4, and N >= 3, Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN) with an Information Component (IC025) > 0, and Multi-Gamma Poisson Shrinkage (MGPS) with EBGM05 >= 2.

The study used publicly available, anonymized data from the FAERS database and qualified for exemption from ethics committee approval, complying with the FDA's FAERS data use policies and applicable privacy regulations.

The final dataset included 7,244 PML reports involving 298 drugs, with an overall mean patient age of 53.8 ± 15.6 years, mean body weight of 70.4 ± 18.8 kg, and a male-to-female ratio of approximately 1:1.3.
The pharmacovigilance analysis identified 72 drugs showing disproportionate PML reporting patterns using four independent signal detection algorithms.

The study calculated reporting odds ratios (RORs) with 95% confidence intervals for the identified agents, with ROR values ranging from 2.91 (95% CI: 2.04-4.17) for ofatumumab to 40.42 (95% CI: 24.65-66.26) for chlorambucil.

The study utilized the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, including spontaneously reported adverse drug event records worldwide from the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) reports were identified using the MedDRA Preferred Term "Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy" and validated through review of narrative fields and supporting documentation by two independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer.
Reports with incomplete information or where PML could not be confirmed were excluded from the analysis.

All drugs were standardized to International Nonproprietary Names (INN), and vaccines, diagnostic agents, combination preparations, herbal medicines, and records with unclear drug indications were excluded.

Indications were categorized based on the MedDRA classification system into major underlying disease groups, and for reports with multiple indications, the primary underlying disease was determined based on the reported indication for the suspected causative drug, clinical context, and medical literature.

Four pharmacovigilance signal detection methods were jointly applied: frequentist disproportionality measures Relative Odds Ratio (ROR) and Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), and Bayesian shrinkage approaches Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN) and Multi-Gamma Prior Shrinkage (MGPS).
The study required concordant signals across all four methods to prioritize specificity and reduce spurious findings due to random variation, acknowledging a potential loss of sensitivity.
The inclusion criteria for Relative Odds Ratio (ROR) were ROR > 1 and a 95% confidence interval lower bound > 1.
The inclusion criteria for Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR) were PRR > 2, chi-square > 4, and N >= 3.
The inclusion criteria for Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN) were an Information Component (IC025) > 0.
The inclusion criteria for Multi-Gamma Prior Shrinkage (MGPS) were an Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (EBGM05) >= 2.

The study systematically analyzed the epidemiological characteristics, drug signals, and clinical risk factors of drug-associated progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) using the FAERS database for the period from 2004 to 2024.
The geographic distribution map of PML reports was created by the authors using Datawrapper software with a public-domain base map from Natural Earth.
The study applied multiple signal-detection methods to the FAERS database to identify 72 drugs with strong PML signals.

The study utilized the FAERS database to perform drug signal detection for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, as depicted in the process diagram in Figure 1. The analysis identified the top 30 drugs showing positive signals across four specific detection algorithms: Reporting Odds Ratio, Proportional Reporting Ratio, Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean, and Information Component.

The statistical analysis employed four specific algorithms with defined parameters: Reporting Odds Ratio (95% Confidence Interval), Proportional Reporting Ratio (Chi-square), Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (5th percentile of posterior distribution), and Information Component (2.5th percentile of posterior distribution). The study selected the top 30 drugs from a total of 72 drugs that showed positive signals in all four of these detection algorithms.

The study analyzed the time-to-onset (TTO) from drug initiation to PML reporting for the top 10 signal-positive drugs out of the 72 total identified. The median TTO values were calculated for these drugs, with natalizumab showing a median of 262 days and rituximab showing a median of 335 days.
The study utilized the FAERS database, which is US-centric and may affect case confirmation and reporting completeness due to reliance on MRI and cerebrospinal fluid JCV PCR for diagnosis.

Most reports in the FAERS database come from healthcare professionals, which enhances the reliability of the data compared to spontaneous reporting systems that rely primarily on patient self-reporting.

The study employed four mainstream signal detection methods (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS) and included only drugs identified as positive by all four methods to determine risk drugs associated with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).

The analysis relied on the FAERS database, which is subject to reporting bias, missing data, and unmeasured confounding, meaning the findings represent disproportionality signals rather than causal inference or absolute incidence.
The study utilized data from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), a passive surveillance system that does not provide incidence estimates.

The analysis sought to explain high-signal drug-PML associations by evaluating plausible pathogenic mechanisms, specifically focusing on immunomodulators such as rituximab and natalizumab that act on B and T cells.
The study identified that natalizumab and rituximab ranked in the top two by Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) for PML associations.

The methodological interpretation of CD4+ T lymphocyte assessment adopted a multidimensional strategy that considered CD4 counts, bioenergetic status (intracellular ATP concentration), and functional subsets, rather than relying on CD4 counts alone.

The study systematically analyzed drug-associated PML reporting patterns using the FAERS database, a spontaneous reporting system where data incompleteness and reporting biases can significantly impact time-to-event estimates.
The study cohort exhibited heterogeneity in baseline diseases, including multiple sclerosis, lymphoma, autoimmune diseases, and organ transplantation, which likely influenced the timing of PML onset.

The study utilized FAERS data, which cannot effectively disentangle drug effects from baseline risk factors such as underlying indication, disease severity, and concomitant immunosuppression, nor distinguish between therapeutic drugs and causative drugs. This limitation means the reported signals are considered hypothesis-generating rather than causal evidence.

The study analyzed the median time to onset (TTO) of major drugs and observed substantial heterogeneity in reported TTO, ranging from 49 days to 1343 days (approximately 1.6 to 44.8 months). These findings differ from Maas's study, which reported an average TTO of 29.5 months with subgroups ranging from 14.2 to 37.8 months.

The study utilized the FAERS spontaneous reporting system, which has inherent flaws including underreporting, incomplete information, and selection bias that may lead to underestimation or overestimation of certain signals.

The study dataset lacked key clinical variables such as concomitant medications, detailed underlying conditions, and treatment dosage and duration, with time-to-onset potentially underestimating true cumulative exposure.

The detected signals in the study mix potential drug-PML associations with the background PML risk conferred by underlying indications like HIV/AIDS and lymphoma, making confounding by indication difficult to disentangle.
The study employed multiple signal detection methods to enhance reliability, but differences in sensitivity and specificity across these methods may lead to inconsistencies in results.
The study utilized the public version of the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database for data mining.
The analysis employed empirical Bayes data mining methods to evaluate drug interactions and detect adverse drug reactions.
The study used proportional reporting ratios (PRRs) for signal generation from spontaneous adverse drug reaction reports.
The study performed a disproportionality analysis of the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) adverse event reporting system (FAERS) events.
The study conducted a pharmacovigilance investigation based on the FDA adverse event reporting system.
The study performed a real-world disproportionality analysis of the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) adverse event reporting system (FAERS) events for Durvalumab.
The study conducted a safety assessment of brexanolone in the FAERS database using real adverse event analysis.
The study was a real-world pharmacovigilance study of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis from the FAERS database.

The study utilized a cross-sectional design with a sample size of n = 100 patients and lacked longitudinal data, which methodologically precludes establishing temporal precedence or distinguishing whether macrophage activation drives disability or if both are independent markers of chronic disease burden.

The correlation models failed to adequately control for age and disease duration, introducing a significant confounding effect that threatens the validity of the reported effect sizes and prevents the isolation of specific retinal biomarker contributions.

The analysis examined six biomarkers without applying adjustments for multiple comparisons, which inflates the Type I error rate and renders borderline p-values unreliable for supporting standalone biomarker claims.

The correlation between the 25-foot walk trial and the retinal metric was negligible at r = 0.034, while the broader correlation of interest was r = 0.196, indicating that the wide confidence intervals and low effect sizes do not support the data as a standalone biomarker.
The retinal study's correlation models were not corrected for multiple comparisons, a methodological omission that renders the reported correlations statistically indistinguishable from noise.

The study utilized a cross-sectional design, which is methodologically insufficient to support the inferential leap from a lack of evidence for a specific neuroinflammatory mechanism to evidence for secondary degeneration.

The animal model study employed a cuprizone model, a methodological choice that fails to recapitulate the heterogeneous and chronic pathology of human MS, thereby limiting the translational validity of the robust effect sizes and tight confidence intervals observed.

The animal model study's reproducibility is compromised by the methodological choice to exclude mice that failed the VEP trial, which introduces selection bias, and by the omission of specific stimulus parameters in the reported data.

The FAERS analysis is fully reproducible because the public dashboard and supplementary files provide all necessary data, and the study design requires concordance across four methods to prioritize specificity in identifying potential safety signals.

The FAERS analysis is the only fully reproducible component because the public dashboard and supplementary files provide all necessary data, whereas the retinal study remains stalled due to the absence of shared code for uncontrolled covariates that prevents independent verification of reported effect sizes.

The animal model's mechanistic findings are currently unverifiable and lack generalizability to human pathophysiology because the exact ESPION stimulus parameters, software versions, and calibration details required for reproducibility were not provided.

The study design comparing RR-MS patients (n=92) to progressive cases (n=3) is statistically underpowered and relies on uncorrected p-values, specifically a p=0.020 for MLC density differences between EDSS groups, which prevents the translation of these findings into a reliable clinical biomarker.

Resolving the current methodological opacity requires a prospective controlled trial with n > 200 per exposure group, powered to detect a hazard ratio of 1.5 with 80% power, to move beyond the current uncorrected p-value of .038 and verify the link between specific drugs and PML risk.

documents: The study utilized a novel, selective GPR17 antagonist administered orally to cuprizone-induced murine demyelination models to evaluate effects on remyelination.
All relevant data for the study are contained within the paper and its Supporting Information files.
The research was funded by Rewind Therapeutics NV, Leuven, a for-profit organization.

The study utilized the synthetic small molecule ligand MDL-29951, described as the most selective and specific GPR17 agonist identified to date, to demonstrate the competitive antagonism of RWT020016.

GPR17 remains classified as an orphan receptor because reproducibility efforts failed to confirm the activity of cysteinyl leukotrienes, purines, and 24(S)-hydroxycholesterol (24S-HC), and independent validation of the cytokine C1q as a ligand is lacking.

Spatial working memory was assessed using the spontaneous Y-maze alternation task at week 6 and week 12 for the acute cuprizone model and week 7 and week 17 for the chronic cuprizone model. Each mouse was placed in a Y-maze arm and allowed to freely explore for a total of 6 minutes, with an arm entry recorded when both hind paws fully entered an arm.

A correct triad was defined as a sequence of consecutive entries into three different arms, and the primary measure of spatial working memory was the percentage of spontaneous alternation calculated using the formula: (Number of correct triads / (total arm entries - 2)) * 100. Mice that failed to complete at least five triads during the 6-minute trial were excluded from analysis due to insufficient exploration.

Mouse optic nerves were fixed at week 17 of the chronic cuprizone study following a lethal injection of 200 mg/kg pentobarbital and cardiac perfusion. The optic nerves were immersed overnight at 4°C in 2% glutaraldehyde in 0.05 M sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 7.3), washed in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer, and post-fixed in 2% osmium tetroxide in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer for 60 minutes.

Five images of optic nerve sections per mouse were randomly selected and analyzed in a blinded manner using Fiji ImageJ software. The g-ratio was calculated as the ratio of the inner axonal diameter to the total outer diameter of the myelinated fiber, measuring 25 axons per image.

A reference value for normal mitochondrial density was established from a pilot study (n=5) as an average of 0.15/μm² (equivalent to 30 per 200 μm²), derived from assessing the numerical density of axons containing mitochondria within 5 images of 200 μm² size per animal. This reference value was used to assess ultrastructural pathology in the current study.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism for Windows version 10.2.1, with data presented as mean values plus or minus standard error of the mean (SEM) and a significance threshold of p < 0.05.
The reference value for normal mitochondrial density was established at an average of 0.15 per square micrometer, which is equivalent to 30 mitochondria per 200 square micrometers.

The cumulative pathology score for optic nerve images is calculated by adding one point for each of six specific features: altered mitochondrial morphology, higher density of altered mitochondria, loose myelin sheaths, empty or swollen axons, degenerating axons with cellular or membranous debris, and fully degenerated axons with only myelin debris remaining.
Samples are classified into four grades based on the average score per optic nerve: grade 1 for scores of 2-3, grade 2 for scores of 3-4, grade 3 for scores of 4-5, and grade 4 for scores of 5-6.

The study utilized a mechanistic de- and remyelination model that does not recapitulate the full inflammatory complexity of demyelinating diseases, which is a gap for replicating therapeutic strategies targeting inflammation.

Transmission electron microscopy analysis of the optic nerve quantified G-ratios of 125 axons per optic nerve from five TEM images per optic nerve section, with a sample size of N=6 per group. The compound RWT020016 inhibits GPR17 signaling to release the differentiation block of committed oligodendrocyte precursor cells (COPs), allowing progression to mature myelin-forming oligodendrocytes (MFOLs).
The proposed mechanism for RWT020016-mediated remyelination involves enhanced lactate release, increased lipid biosynthesis, and elevated myelin basic protein (MBP) expression.

The study utilized the cuprizone mouse model and assessed myelin thickness using G-ratio analysis, alongside a qualitative structural analysis integrating mitochondrial morphology, axonal and myelin integrity.

A gap in replication exists because larger sample sizes are required for formal statistical comparisons at the ultrastructural level, and expanded morphometric analysis is needed to strengthen the data on g-ratios and axonal integrity.

The study focused exclusively on male mice to reduce biological variability, which limits the generalizability of the findings and requires future studies to include both sexes to assess sex-dependent differences in pharmacokinetics and remyelination efficacy.

Replication is blocked by the lack of additional ultrastructural investigations in the corpus callosum and the absence of immunohistochemical and volumetric cellular density analyses using markers of mature oligodendrocytes to confirm GPR17 function blocking.

A gap in target engagement assessment exists because GPR17 expression does not undergo autoregulatory feedback, and direct assessment of downstream signaling events in GPR17-expressing cells is required instead of quantifying GPR17+ cell density.

The study's claim to confirm the 2022 biological mechanism is blocked by the unavailability of raw logs, which are required to rule out novelty effects as a confounder for the observed symptom reduction.
Replication of the statistical analysis is impeded by the lack of access to raw logs, preventing verification of whether pre-processing steps were consistent across the data split.

The primary statistical threat to the study's validity is an uncorrected p-value of .038 accompanied by an effect size near zero, which undermines the claim of a definitive biological pathway confirmation.

The study's computational pipeline is non-reproducible because the methods section omits the specific software versions used for the data split and randomization steps, preventing verification of pipeline stability.

Replication is blocked by uncontrolled biological heterogeneity in the post-mortem samples, specifically post-mortem delays ranging from 7 to 10 hours and brain weights varying from 998 to 1390 grams.

Inclusion criteria for multiple sclerosis patients required a diagnosis per the 2017 McDonald criteria, an age between 18 and 60 years, and a brain MRI with or without contrast performed within the preceding 12 months. Exclusion criteria for multiple sclerosis patients included ophthalmologic or systemic disorders affecting the retina, previous history of optic neuritis, or incomplete medical release during enrollment.

Inclusion criteria for healthy controls required an age between 18 and 60 years, normal MRI findings, no history of uveitis or vitreoretinal pathology, and no personal or family history of multiple sclerosis.
