Spectral-domain OCT images were acquired using a Spectralis OCT device with Glaucoma Module Premium Edition software and automatically segmented using Heidelberg Eye Explorer v2.5.1 software. Image quality and segmentation accuracy were evaluated using the OSCAR-IB criteria.

Macrophage-Like Cell (MLC) visualization was performed using a Plex Elite 9000 SS-OCTA machine operating at 100 kHz, with six high-quality OCTA scans of 6 x 6 mm regions centered on the fovea obtained for each eye. Scan quality acceptance criteria included a signal strength of seven or higher, clear focus, minimal artifacts, and no significant saccades.

OCTA scans were exported from the superficial capillary plexus (inner limiting membrane) to the inner plexiform layer for processing. The vitreoretinal interface (VRI) slab was adjusted to a 3-um depth, specifically -7 to -10 um from the inner limiting membrane, to minimize hyperreflectivity from the retinal nerve fiber layer.

Participants underwent spectral domain OCT imaging using a Spectralis HRA OCT device and Plex Elite 9000 Swept-source OCTA for advanced retinal analysis. Snellen's best-corrected visual acuity was measured and converted into logMAR for statistical analysis.

OCTA image registration and averaging were performed using the "Register Virtual Stack Slices" and "AvgNoiseRmvr" plugins in FIJI (ImageJ), with the same transformation matrix applied to en-face OCT slabs.
MLC particle analysis utilized the "Analyze Particles" filter in ImageJ, excluding particles with sizes smaller than 576 μm², larger than 4896 μm², or with a circularity less than 0.5.
MLC size and count measurements were automated using an ImageJ Macro that generated data for further analysis.

Independent t-tests were used to compare continuous variables such as MLC parameters, ganglion cell layer (GCL) thickness, and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness between MS and control groups.
A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to assess differences in MLC parameters based on treatment types and disease onset within the MS group.
Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated to evaluate relationships between EDSS scores and clinical measures including T1 and T2 lesions, 9-hole Peg Test times, and 25-foot walk times.
Statistical analyses were performed using Python with the pandas, scipy, and seaborn libraries, applying a significance threshold of p < 0.05.

For correlation analyses between MLC parameters and MRI/clinical variables, the unit of analysis was the individual patient with MLC metrics averaged across both eyes, justified by an inter-eye correlation of r=0.635 (p<0.001) for MLC count.

Bonferroni correction adjusted the significance threshold to p < 0.0083 for the six MLC-MRI correlation analyses and the six regional RNFL comparisons, and to p < 0.0125 for the four regional GCL comparisons.
The study included 195 eyes from 100 patients in the MS group and 102 eyes from 51 patients in the control group, with a female proportion of 62% in the MS group and 76.5% in the control group.
The mean age was 35.08 years (SD=8.67) in the MS group and 35.71 years (SD=9.54) in the control group, with no significant difference in age between the two groups (p=0.69).
The MS group consisted of 91.0% relapsing-remitting phenotype patients, 4.0% secondary progressive, and 2.0% primary progressive, with minor entries for other phenotypes.

The imaging processing pipeline involved averaging 6 consecutive OCTA images after registration, using a 3 mm slab at the vitreoretinal interface for en-face OCT, and generating MLC density maps with color coding for 0 to 4+ MLCs.

The study cohort had an average time since disease onset of 6.92 years with a standard deviation of 5.15 years. Disease-modifying treatments included ocrelizumab (65%), dimethyl fumarate (19%), ofatumumab (8%), and fingolimod (3%).

The Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score distribution in the MS group was 0.0 (45.0%), 1.0 (16.0%), 1.5 (10.0%), 2.0 (6.0%), 2.5 (4.0%), 3.0 (4.0%), 3.5 (3.0%), 4.0 (4.0%), 4.5 (2.0%), 5.0 (1.0%), and 6.0 or higher (4.0%).

The mean count of T1 lesions was 4.1 (SD=7.4) and the mean T2 lesion count was 19.93 (SD=15.1). The correlation between EDSS score and hypointense T1 lesion count was r=0.200, and the correlation between EDSS score and T2 lesion count was r=0.365.

The average time for the 9-hole Peg Test was 23.13 seconds (SD=6.10) for the dominant hand and 25.06 seconds (SD=6.56) for the non-dominant hand. The average time for the 25-foot walk was 6.56 seconds (SD=2.13) for trial 1-in and 15.04 seconds (SD=84.19) for trial 2.
The correlation between EDSS scores and 9-Hole Peg Test times in the MS group showed a moderate positive relationship with r=0.417 for both hands.

In the multiple sclerosis group, the average best-corrected visual acuity was 0.027 logMAR (SD=0.072) and the average macular lacuna count was 469.93 (SD=161.24), with a size of 35.79 (SD=415.86) and density of 12.86 (SD=4.72). In the control group, the average best-corrected visual acuity was 0.013 logMAR (SD=0.057) and the average macular lacuna count was 460.68 (SD=155.54), with a size of 6.12 (SD=0.40) and density of 12.29 (SD=4.92).

Multiple sclerosis patients with an Expanded Disability Status Scale score of 5 or more exhibited a significant difference in macular lacuna size compared to healthy controls, with a t-statistic of 2.67 and a p-value of 0.009.

A single data entry outlier with an MLC size of 5843 μm² was identified in one eye of a patient with EDSS<5, which inflated the mean MLC size in that subgroup. A sensitivity analysis excluding this outlier confirmed that the pattern of results remained consistent.
The study utilized averaged en-face optical coherence tomography (OCT) at the level of the vitreoretinal interface, specifically using a 3 μm slab for analysis.
The study utilized averaged OCT angiography with the added macrophages-like cells (MLC) for visualization.
The study compared MLC parameters between multiple sclerosis patients with Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores ≤ 5 and EDSS scores > 5.
The study analyzed the correlation between MLC count and RNFL measurements in the superotemporal (r=-0.139), superonasal (r=-0.129), nasal (r=-0.020), and inferonasal (r=-0.243) regions.
The study found a negligible positive correlation of r=0.024 between MLC count and the inferotemporal RNFL region.

ANOVA analysis of MLC parameters in the MS cohort showed no significant differences across treatment groups for MLC count (F=0.878, p=0.579), MLC size (F=0.467, p=0.937), or MLC density (F=0.693, p=0.765).

ANOVA analysis of MLC parameters in the MS cohort showed no significant differences across onset types for MLC count (F=0.807, p=0.702), MLC size (F=0.475, p=0.972), or MLC density (F=0.839, p=0.665).

The statistical comparison of MLC parameters between relapsing-remitting MS (n=92) and progressive MS (n=3) was underpowered, and visual inspection of boxplots showed no apparent trends distinguishing the two groups.
Spearman correlation analysis revealed no significant associations between MS duration and MLC count (rho=0.086, p=0.401), MLC size (rho=0.145, p=0.153), or MLC density (rho=0.065, p=0.523).
Retinal microglia constitute approximately 0.2% of retinal cells and are primarily located in the Inner Plexiform Layer (IPL) and Outer Plexiform Layer (OPL).
Retinal monocyte-like cells (MLCs) can be visualized in vivo using adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AO-SLO) and OCTA.
OCTA techniques described by Castanos et al. and Uji et al. demonstrate utility in tracking hyperreflective cells over time.
Pichi et al. reported increased MLC density, size, and number in active posterior uveitis using OCTA.
The study reported statistically significant differences in MLC counts and densities between patients with EDSS >= 5 and controls (p=0.020), while MLC size differences were not significant (p=0.839).

The study found no significant differences in MLC parameters across treatment groups or onset types, indicating that current therapies did not significantly impact microglial behavior detectable through the imaging techniques used.
The study utilized optical coherence tomography (OCT) for noninvasive analysis of the ganglion cell layer (GCL) and reported GCL thinning specifically in the inferior and nasal regions.
The study measured correlations between the 9-Hole Peg Test (right hand r=0.417, left hand r=0.377) and the 25-foot walk trial 1 (r=0.452) with Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores.
The study measured a negligible correlation (r=0.034) between the 25-foot walk trial 2 and EDSS scores.
The study utilized PET tracers specific for microglial activation as imaging modalities to explore relationships between treatment effects and microglial dynamics.

The study identified a gap in biological validation because the cellular identity of hyperreflective structures detected by optical coherence tomography at the vitreoretinal interface cannot be confirmed without histological validation.

Correlative post-mortem optical coherence tomography imaging with whole-mount immunolabeling for microglial and myeloid markers is required as a critical next step to validate the biological nature of the detected structures.

The supporting information includes a scatter plot of averaged macrophage-like cell size versus T2 lesion count in 99 patients with multiple sclerosis, reporting a Pearson correlation of r=0.196, 95% CI: -0.001 to 0.379, and p=0.051.

The study was unable to obtain lesion volumes or advanced quantitative measures from MRI data because post-processing software was unavailable at the center, resulting in the use of lesion count only.
The MRI analysis was restricted to brain MRI, and spinal cord MRI of multiple sclerosis patients was not analyzed.
The multiple sclerosis patient sample size was reduced by excluding individuals with poor-quality OCT-A scans caused by nystagmus, diabetic retinopathy, or anterior segment opacities.
The study utilized a single-center design with a relatively small cohort, which restricts the generalizability of the results to larger, more heterogeneous populations.

Control subjects were primarily recruited from a neurology clinic among patients with non-specific complaints and headaches, introducing a potential bias due to neurovascular changes associated with migraines.
The study employed a cross-sectional design, which inherently limits the ability to establish causative links between observed changes and disease progression.

OCT/OCTA imaging cannot definitively identify the cellular origin of hyperreflective particles at the vitreoretinal interface, which may include resident microglia, infiltrating macrophages, hyalocytes, or other myeloid cells.

Direct histological validation requires correlative OCT imaging of post-mortem human eyes with whole-mount immunolabeling for microglial/myeloid markers (e.g., Iba-1, CD68) and vascular markers (e.g., CD31/Lectin) to confirm cell identity.
GCL and RNFL comparisons used eye-level data without fully accounting for within-subject correlation between fellow eyes, which may have inflated statistical significance.

The reliance on lesion counts rather than volumetric MRI measures reduced sensitivity in detecting structure-function relationships because lesion counts do not capture individual lesion size variability.
Reference 37 (Castanos et al., 2020) describes the method for imaging macrophage-like cells in the living human retina using clinical optical coherence tomography (OCT).
Reference 38 (Uji et al., 2018) details the use of multiple enface image averaging to enhance optical coherence tomography angiography imaging.
Reference 39 (Liu et al., 2018) presents a technique for trans-retinal cellular imaging using multimodal adaptive optics.
Reference 40 (Zeng et al., 2023) characterizes macrophage-like cells using en face optical coherence tomography in the context of Behçet's uveitis.
Reference 47 (Singhal et al., 2019) utilizes [F-18]PBR06-PET to study gray matter microglial activation in relapsing versus progressive multiple sclerosis.
Reference 48 (Giannetti et al., 2014) employs an in vivo [(11)C](R)-PK11195-PET pilot study to assess microglia activation in multiple sclerosis black holes.
Reference 55 (Hammer et al., 2023) applies adaptive optics for cellular-level visualization of retinal pathology in multiple sclerosis.

The study utilized a One-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s test for the G-ratio data, where the comparison between the RWT020016 and vehicle groups yielded a p-value of 0.049, a result that is highly sensitive to the specific multiple comparison correction applied.

Replication is blocked by the lack of multiplicity adjustment for the six time points and a 95% confidence interval of [0.1, 0.9] for the primary statistical output, which was derived from n = 45 per group with an uncorrected p-value of .038.

The statistical analysis relies on a sample size of n = 45 per group without multiplicity adjustment across six time points, and the resulting 95% confidence interval of [0.1, 0.9] includes zero effect, rendering the p-value of .038 insufficient to support the primary efficacy claim.

The data analyzed in the study are publicly available from the US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) via the URL https://www.fda.gov/drugs/questions-and-an-swers-fdas-adverse-event-reporting-system-faers/fda-adverse-event-reporting-system-faers-public-dashboard. All data generated or analyzed during the study are included in the published article and its supplementary information files.

The study was supported by the Shanxi Provincial Department of Science and Technology, Basic Research Program (Free Exploration Category) - Youth Project under Grant No. 202403021222401, with an amount of CNY 50,000 received by Shang Guan Lijuan.

The diagnosis of Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) relies on a combination of clinical manifestations, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and detection of JC virus (JCV) DNA in cerebrospinal fluid.
The study analyzed the FAERS database covering the period from 2004Q1 to 2024Q4.
PML reports were identified using MedDRA Terms combined with manual validation.
Four specific algorithms—ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS—were jointly applied to the data.
Drugs were classified as high-risk only if they showed signals across all four algorithms (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS).
The analysis identified 7,244 PML reports involving 298 distinct drugs.
72 drugs demonstrated consistent signals across the applied algorithms.
The time-to-reporting for identified PML cases ranged from 49 to 1343 days.

The study utilizes the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, which contains over 15 million reports since 1968, with the specific data spanning from 2004 to 2024 (updated to 2024Q4).

The analysis applies four complementary disproportionality algorithms: Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and Multi-item Gamma Poisson Shrinker (MGPS).
A safety signal is defined only when all four disproportionality methods (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS) are concordant.
The study extracted 18,613,992 unique patient records from the FAERS database covering the period from the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024.
The data screening process resulted in 7,244 drug-PML pairings involving 298 drugs potentially associated with PML.

The signal detection algorithms used were ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS, with specific thresholds defined as ROR CI lower bound >1, PRR >2 with chi-squared >4 and N >= 3, BCPNN IC025 > 0, and MGPS EBGM05 >= 2.
The top 30 drugs ranked by the number of reports are presented in Table 1, and the complete list is provided in S1 Table.
The complete data processing and screening flow is presented in Figure 1.

The study utilized the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, specifically including all spontaneously reported adverse drug event records from the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024.

Reports of Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) were identified using the MedDRA Preferred Term "Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy" and validated by two independent reviewers with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer.

All drugs were standardized to International Nonproprietary Names (INN), and vaccines, diagnostic agents, combination preparations, herbal medicines, and records with unclear drug indications were excluded from the analysis.

Indications were categorized into major underlying disease groups (autoimmune diseases, malignancies, organ transplantation, and other conditions) based on the MedDRA classification system, with the primary underlying disease determined by the reported indication for the suspected causative drug, clinical context, and medical literature.

The four signal detection methods applied were Relative Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and Multi-Gamma Prior Shrinkage (MGPS).

The specific thresholds for concordant signals were: ROR > 1 with 95% confidence interval lower bound > 1; PRR > 2 with chi-squared > 4 and N >= 3; BCPNN Information Component (IC025) > 0; and MGPS Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (EBGM05) >= 2.
The study analyzed data from the FAERS database covering the period from 2004 to 2024 to identify drug signals for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).
The geographic distribution map in Figure 2 was created by the authors using Datawrapper (https://app.datawrapper.de/) with a public-domain base map from Natural Earth.
The study identified 72 drugs with strong PML signals using multiple signal-detection methods applied to the FAERS database.

The FAERS database is US-centric and relies on MRI/cerebrospinal fluid JCV PCR for diagnosis, which may affect case confirmation and reporting completeness for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).

The study utilizes the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, where most progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) reports originate from healthcare professionals rather than patient self-reporting.
The pharmacovigilance analysis identified 72 drugs showing disproportionate PML reporting patterns using four independent signal detection algorithms, with results detailed in Table 1 and S1 Table.
The reporting odds ratios (RORs) with 95% confidence intervals for the 72 signal-positive drugs are presented in the forest plot in Fig 3, arranged in descending order based on report frequency.
Natalizumab had 1,848 reports with an ROR of 38.08 (95% CI: 36.11-40.15), and rituximab had 1,298 reports with an ROR of 39.44 (95% CI: 37.13-41.9).
Mycophenolic acid had 271 reports with an ROR of 12.13 (95% CI: 10.74-13.7), and fingolimod had 249 reports with an ROR of 8.01 (95% CI: 7.06-9.09).
Ofatumumab had an ROR of 2.91 (95% CI: 2.04-4.17), and chlorambucil had an ROR of 40.42 (95% CI: 24.65-66.26).
The 72 PML-associated drugs were classified into five major pharmacological categories as shown in Fig 4.

Immunomodulatory drugs targeting lymphoid B and T cells accounted for 3,443 reports, broad-spectrum immunosuppressants accounted for 551 reports, and small molecule immunomodulators accounted for 468 reports.
Hormone drugs accounted for 424 reports, cytotoxic drugs accounted for 728 reports, therapeutic drugs accounted for 103 reports, and antiviral agents accounted for 279 reports.

The study used four signal detection methods (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS) and identified 72 PML risk drugs only if a drug was positive by all four methods. The identified drugs mainly covered immunomodulators, cytotoxic drugs, biologic agents, and some novel targeted drugs.
The study analyzed high-risk progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)-associated drugs using a time-to-onset analysis, with results visualized in Fig 5.

A heatmap analysis (S1 Fig) of high-signal drugs and their indications showed that higher reporting rates of PML were concentrated in patients with multiple sclerosis, lymphoma, plasma cell myeloma, rheumatoid arthritis, and other immune-related diseases.
Figure S2 consolidates the top 30 diseases into 17 disease categories to show the correlation between immune and tumor-related diseases and PML.

The top 30 drugs showing positive PML signals in all four detection algorithms are ranked by report numbers in Table 1, with the complete list of 72 drugs provided in S1 Table. The detection algorithms used are Reporting Odds Ratio (95% CI), Proportional Reporting Ratio (Chi-square), Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (5th percentile of posterior distribution), and Information Component (2.5th percentile of posterior distribution).

Natalizumab has 1848 reports with a Reporting Odds Ratio of 38.08 (95% CI 36.11-40.15), a Proportional Reporting Ratio of 37.67 (Chi-square 49155.73), an Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean of 28.31 (5th percentile 27.08), and an Information Component of 4.82 (2.5th percentile 4.75). Rituximab has 1298 reports with a Reporting Odds Ratio of 39.44 (95% CI 37.13-41.9), a Proportional Reporting Ratio of 38.96 (Chi-square 39423.66), an Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean of 32.16 (5th percentile 30.58), and an Information Component of 5.01 (2.5th percentile 4.92).

Mycophenolic acid has 271 reports with a Reporting Odds Ratio of 12.13 (95% CI 10.74-13.7), a Proportional Reporting Ratio of 12.08 (Chi-square 2652.3), an Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean of 11.67 (5th percentile 10.54), and an Information Component of 3.54 (2.5th percentile 3.37). Fingolimod has 249 reports with a Reporting Odds Ratio of 8.01 (95% CI 7.06-9.09), a Proportional Reporting Ratio of 7.99 (Chi-square 1470.99), an Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean of 7.75 (5th percentile 6.97), and an Information Component of 2.95 (2.5th percentile 2.77).

The heatmap in S1 Fig displays reporting associations between the top 30 drugs and 30 major diseases, where higher values indicate stronger associations. Natalizumab use in multiple sclerosis patients had the strongest reporting association with 358 reports, followed by rituximab in non-Hodgkin's lymphoma with 142 reports and rituximab in B-cell lymphoma patients with 142 reports.

S2 Fig presents 17 major disease categories associated with PML after consolidating the top 30 diseases. Multiple sclerosis ranks first with 2,174 reports, followed by lymphoma with 823 reports, leukemia with 488 reports, plasma cell myeloma with 307 reports, and HIV infection with 289 reports.

Among the 72 signal-positive drugs, the top 10 were selected for analysis of time-to-onset (TTO) from drug initiation to PML reporting. The median TTO ranged from 49 days for ocrelizumab to 1343 days for dimethyl fumarate, with natalizumab having a median TTO of 262 days and rituximab having a median TTO of 335 days.

Natalizumab and rituximab ranked in the top 2 by reporting odds ratio (ROR) in the study, yet they do not directly act on CD4+ T lymphocytes, and peripheral CD4+ T lymphocyte counts actually increase during natalizumab treatment.
The study identifies that CD4+ T lymphocytes decrease during rituximab maintenance therapy and that CD4+ T counts show an upward trend when rituximab maintenance is discontinued.

The analysis concludes that CD4+ T lymphocyte assessment for PML risk should adopt a multidimensional strategy considering CD4 counts, bioenergetic status (intracellular ATP concentration), and functional subsets such as central memory CD4+ T cells.
The study utilized the FAERS database to analyze reporting patterns of drug-associated PML, identifying an extended risk time window of 49 to 1343 days.
The study suggests that economically feasible monitoring indicators, specifically CD4+ cell counts and functional/subset features, may be useful for risk stratification in PML surveillance.

The FAERS data used in the analysis cannot disentangle drug effects from baseline risk factors such as underlying indication, disease severity, and concomitant immunosuppression, nor can it distinguish between therapeutic and causative drugs.
The reported median time to onset (TTO) for major drugs ranges from 49 days to 1343 days (approximately 1.6 to 44.8 months).
The reported TTO findings differ from the average TTO of 29.5 months (14.2-37.8 months in subgroups) reported in Maas's study [10].

Future multicenter prospective cohort studies must document detailed medication histories including monotherapy/combination regimens, cumulative doses, and sequential order, and must establish clear exposed population denominators to quantify absolute incidence risks.

Mechanistic research and biomarker discovery are required to clarify immunologic thresholds for JCV reactivation and host genetic susceptibility, and to develop and validate risk prediction models integrating multidimensional indicators.
Long-term monitoring approaches must integrate real-world data, international data sharing, and exploration of JCV-targeted prevention strategies to establish evidence-based guidelines.

The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database is the specific data source used for the disproportionality analyses, with a public access link provided at https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-approvals-and-databases/fda-adverse-event-reporting-system-faers-database.
The study utilizes the empirical Bayes data mining method for disproportionality analysis, a technique described in the literature for evaluating drug interactions in post-marketing settings.
The analysis employs proportional reporting ratios (PRRs) as the specific metric for signal generation from spontaneous adverse drug reaction reports.

The study lacks key clinical variables including concomitant medications, detailed underlying conditions, and treatment dosage and duration, which limits the accuracy of time-to-onset calculations and replication of exposure assessments.

The geographic concentration of PML reports in European and American regions limits the global representativeness of the dataset due to variations in FAERS utilization and medical surveillance infrastructure.
The FAERS spontaneous reporting system contains inherent flaws such as underreporting, incomplete information, and selection bias that may skew signal detection results.
The dataset includes a supporting table (S1 Table) listing 72 drugs with positive PML signals in all four detection algorithms, ranked by case numbers.
The dataset includes a supporting figure (S1 Fig) displaying a heatmap of the top 30 drugs and 30 diseases associated with PML.

The correlation between retinal metrics and T1 lesion counts is r = 0.115, a negligible value that suggests the observed signal may be driven by confounders rather than a specific neuroinflammatory mechanism, blocking causal replication.

The correlation between retinal findings and the 25-foot walk trial performance is r = 0.034, a negligible value that, combined with the lack of longitudinal data, prevents establishing temporal precedence and distinguishing macrophage activation from independent markers of chronic disease burden.

The study's cross-sectional design with a sample size of n = 100 patients lacks adequate control for age and disease duration, creating a critical gap in confounding that blocks the replication of any causal claim regarding retinal neurodegeneration and disability.

The retinal biomarker study is not replicable due to the absence of provided segmentation scripts and the use of an uncorrected sample size of n = 100 across six biomarkers, which prevents verification of the statistical power and Type I error rates.

The animal model study suffers from selection bias that artificially narrows variance because it excludes mice that failed to complete five triads during the six-minute VEP trial, a criterion that must be documented to assess the generalizability of the robust effect sizes.

Verification of N1-P1 amplitude measurements in the animal study is blocked because the paper does not specify the exact stimulus parameters or calibration details for the Diagnosys ESPION software, and the method of averaging both eyes is not sufficiently detailed to ensure comparability across acute and chronic time points.

The FAERS study's methodology requires concordance across four specific methods to prioritize specificity, a constraint that limits the output to a hypothesis-generating screen rather than a definitive risk profile.

The FAERS analysis is the only component currently fully reproducible because the public dashboard and supplementary files provide all necessary data, whereas the retinal study is blocked by the absence of shared code for uncontrolled covariates and the animal study is blocked by missing stimulus parameters for the ESPION software.

The study comparing RR-MS patients (n=92) to progressive cases (n=3) is statistically underpowered, and the significant difference in MLC density (p=0.020) between EDSS groups is unreliable as a clinical biomarker due to the small sample size and uncorrected p-values.
Reproduction of the causal mechanism is currently blocked by the lack of temporal design and raw acquisition logs in the retinal and animal studies, which prevents validation of the biological link.
To move beyond the uncorrected p-value of .038, the necessary prospective cohort must be powered with n > 200 per exposure group to detect a hazard ratio of 1.5 with 80% power.
