documents: The study evaluated RWT020016 efficacy in toxin-induced demyelination mouse models using acute and chronic cuprizone treatments, with functional readouts including visual evoked potentials and a Y-maze test for spatial working memory, and structural readouts including myelin basic protein quantification in the corpus callosum and myelin ultrastructure assessment via transmission electron microscopy in the optic nerve.

Postmortem immunohistochemical analyses of multiple sclerosis patient tissue revealed a significant upregulation of GPR17+/BCAS1+ oligodendrocyte precursor cells adjacent to and in demyelinated lesions.
Remyelinated multiple sclerosis lesions lacked GPR17 immunoreactivity, indicating a lack of GPR17 expression in successfully remyelinated tissue.
Oral treatment with a selective GPR17 antagonist in cuprizone-induced murine demyelination models resulted in improved spatial memory and recovery of visual evoked potential latency delays.

The single-nucleus RNA sequencing meta-analysis utilized five public datasets yielding a total of 214,567 nuclei, which were filtered and integrated to produce a final dataset of 71,623 oligodendrocyte lineage cells.
Dimensionality reduction for the single-nucleus RNA sequencing data was performed using principal component analysis with 7,500 variable features and 75 principal components retained.

Marker genes for clusters and differential expression analyses between oligodendrocyte precursor cell and committed oligodendrocyte precursor populations were identified using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
The qualitative assessment included 3-4 sections per tissue block, with 2-6 visibly distinct lesions evaluated separately per section.

The qualitative immunohistochemical analyses included cerebral tissues and optic nerves from eight donors diagnosed with primary or secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS or SPMS), consisting of two men and six women.

The sample set comprised four donors with cortical lesions (MS-1 to MS-4) and four donors with optic nerve or optic chiasm tissue (MS-5 to MS-8), with postmortem intervals ranging from 07:00 to 10:40 hours and disease durations ranging from 17 to 38 years.

Double immunostaining was performed on sections from all dissected tissue blocks to visualize proteolipid protein (PLP) and human leukocyte antigen (HLA-DR-DQ) for the classification of demyelinating lesions.

The study analyzed 57 female and 53 female postmortem tissue samples from patients with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis and optic neuritis, with postmortem delays of 1145 and 998 minutes respectively.

Cryosectioning involved cutting 8 µm thick coronal sections, fixing them in 4% paraformaldehyde in 1x PBS, and incubating them overnight at 4°C after blocking with 10% normal horse serum, 1% bovine serum albumin, and 0.5% Triton X-100.

Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue processing utilized antigen retrieval in 10 mM Citrate buffer pH 6.0 for GPR17 or 1x TBS pH 7.6 for HLA and PLP, followed by quenching with 1% H2O2 and 0.2% Triton X-100.

Primary antibody dilutions were 1:100 for mouse anti-human HLA-DP, DQ, DR antigen (FFPE) and 1:500 (Cryo), 1:500 for mouse anti-PLP (FFPE) and 1:6000 (Cryo), 1:100 for rabbit anti-GPR17 (FFPE and Cryo), and 1:10,000 for mouse anti-BCAS1 (FFPE and Cryo).

Single-dose pharmacokinetic studies for test compound RWT020016 were conducted with a sample size of N=3 using a dose volume of 5 ml/kg, with plasma and brain homogenate concentrations quantified via a validated LC-MS/MS method.

Pharmacokinetic parameters for RWT020016, including bioavailability, maximum brain concentration, time to maximum brain concentration, terminal half-life, brain area under the concentration-time curve (AUC0-24h), and brain-to-plasma ratios, were calculated using noncompartmental analysis.
cAMP accumulation assays for RWT020016 were performed in CHO-K1 cells stably expressing recombinant murine GPR17, with dose-response curves generated at eight concentrations tested in duplicate.

For RWT020016 antagonist testing, cells were preincubated with the compound for 10 minutes before adding 1 μM forskolin and 200 nM GPR17 agonist MDL-29951, followed by a 30-minute incubation at room temperature.
Calcium mobilization assays used HEK293 cells stably expressing murine or human short GPR17 isoforms, loaded with 20 μL of 0.5x Fluo-8 NW dye per well and incubated for 1 hour at 37 °C.
Cells were treated with RWT020016 in a dose-response format for 20 minutes, followed by stimulation with MDL-29951 at an EC80 concentration of 200 nM.

Selectivity testing utilized human P2Y1, P2Y2, and P2Y11 receptors transiently expressed in 1321N1 cells, and human CysLTR1 transiently expressed in HEK293 cells, with wild-type cell lines serving as negative controls.

Selectivity assays stimulated cells with reference agonists at EC80 concentrations, specifically ATP for P2Y receptors and LTD4 for CysLTR1, after 20 minutes of dose-response treatment with RWT020016.

Control conditions included dose-response treatment with reference antagonists MRS2500 (P2Y1), ARC-118925 XX (P2Y2), Suramin (P2Y11), and Pranlukast (CysLTR1) prior to stimulation with corresponding reference agonists.
Fluorescence signals were recorded in real time and analyzed using Genedata Screener software, with results expressed as a percentage effect relative to normalization standards.
Cuprizone experiments used nine-week-old male C57BL/6OlaHsd mice housed at a controlled temperature of 21-22°C under an inverted light cycle.

The study utilized SPF-grade male C57/BL6J mice maintained under a reverse 12-hour light/dark cycle with controlled temperature (21-22°C). Animals were euthanized with pentobarbital at a dose of 200 mg/kg intraperitoneally.

Cuprizone-induced demyelination was achieved by feeding mice a pelleted diet containing 0.3% (w/w) cuprizone for either 6 weeks (acute model) or 12 weeks (chronic model). Control mice received an identical standard diet without cuprizone.

Mice exhibited an average cuprizone-related body weight loss of 9-15% during the first few days of treatment, with no animal's weight falling below 20% of its baseline value. No animals died or were removed from the acute or chronic cuprizone studies for health-related reasons.

Mice were treated once daily via oral gavage (10 μl/g body weight) for 9 days (acute model) or 37 days (chronic model). The selective GPR17 antagonist RWT020016 was delivered at doses of 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg in a vehicle consisting of 1% (v/v) DMSO, 0.5% (w/v) methylcellulose, and 2% (v/v) Tween 80.

Each mouse was allowed to freely explore the Y-maze for a total of 6 minutes, with arm entries recorded by an experimenter blinded to the condition when both hind paws fully entered an arm. The primary measure of spatial working memory was the percentage of spontaneous alternation, calculated as (Number of correct triads / (total arm entries - 2)) × 100.

Chance performance in the Y-maze corresponds to approximately 50% alternation under the standard triad-based scoring approach, and alternation percentages significantly above 50% were interpreted as evidence of intact working memory. Mice that failed to complete at least five triads during the 6-minute trial were excluded from analysis due to insufficient exploration.
In a pilot study, the numerical density of axons containing mitochondria was assessed within 5 images of 200 μm² size per animal (n=5), yielding an average of 0.15/μm² (equivalent to 30 per 200 μm²).
The g-ratio was calculated as the ratio of the inner axonal diameter to the total outer diameter of the myelinated fiber, with G-ratios measured for 25 axons per image using Fiji (ImageJ).
For each optic nerve, five images of optic nerve sections per mouse were randomly selected and analyzed in a blinded manner using Fiji ImageJ software.

The reference normal mitochondrial density was quantified at an average of $0.15 \mu \mathrm{m}^{2}$, which is equivalent to 30 mitochondria per $200 \mu \mathrm{m}^{2}$. This specific value served as the baseline for comparing mitochondrial density and morphology in the study.

A cumulative pathology score was calculated by adding +1 for each of six specific ultrastructural features, including altered mitochondrial morphology, loose myelin sheaths, and axonal degeneration. The average score per optic nerve classified samples into four grades: grade 1 (score 2-3, none), grade 2 (score 3-4, mild), grade 3 (score 4-5, moderate), and grade 4 (score 5-6, severe).

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism for Windows version 10.2.1, with data presented as mean values ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Differences were considered statistically significant at a threshold of $p<0.05$.
The single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis included a total of 214,567 cells, of which 71,623 were identified as oligodendrocyte lineage cells.
Statistical significance for the differences in the analysis was defined as p<0.05.

No formal quantitative comparisons across lesion types were performed due to limited sample numbers and inter-patient heterogeneity, as such comparisons would not yield statistically robust or biologically meaningful results.
Mice that failed to complete at least five triads during the 6-minute trial were excluded from analysis due to insufficient exploration.

Visual evoked potential (VEP) recordings were performed at baseline, week 6, and week 7 in the acute model, and at week 12 and week 17 in the chronic model, using 200 white light flashes of 310 ms duration at 1 Hz frequency and an intensity of 0.5 cd ⋅ s/m².

Anesthesia for VEP recordings was induced via intraperitoneal injection of 5 μl/g body weight of xylazine (10 mg/kg) and ketamine (70 mg/kg), while pupillary dilation was achieved using 0.5% tropicamide followed by 10% phenylephrine.
N1 VEP latency was measured in milliseconds as the time interval between stimulus onset and cortical response, and N1-P1 amplitude was measured in microvolts to assess axonal damage.
VEP traces were analyzed offline by an experimenter blinded to treatment groups, with values from both eyes of each mouse averaged for statistical analysis.

Mice were perfused intracardially with saline after a 200 mg/kg intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital, and brains were post-fixed overnight in 4% PFA before embedding in optimal cutting temperature medium.

Coronal cryosections of 5 μm thickness were prepared at Bregma -2.0 mm and incubated with rat anti-myelin basic protein (1:500) or rabbit anti-GPR17 (1:200) primary antibodies, followed by anti-rat or anti-rabbit Alexa 555 secondary antibodies (1:400).

A densitometric method using a 32-image format and binary thresholding in ImageJ (Fiji) was used to calculate the percentage area stained for MBP and GPR17 in the medial corpus callosum at Bregma level -2.0 mm.
All immunohistochemistry analyses were performed blinded, and values from cuprizone and treatment groups were expressed relative to the control group.

In the acute (0.3% for 6 weeks) and chronic (0.3% for 12 weeks) cuprizone models, VEP latency showed a significant increase at the end of the demyelination phase (p < 0.0001 vs. control for acute; p < 0.0001 vs. control for chronic), while VEP amplitudes remained comparable to control mice.

At week 6, no significant difference was observed in total arm entries between control and cuprizone-treated mice, whereas at week 12, cuprizone-treated mice showed a significant increase in total arm entries compared with controls (p < 0.0001 vs. control).

Quantitative analysis of MBP expression in the medial corpus callosum revealed a significant reduction in MBP-positive staining after the demyelination phase in both the acute (p < 0.0001 vs. control) and chronic (p < 0.0001 vs. control) cuprizone models.

Visual evoked potential latency was significantly delayed at week 6 in the acute cuprizone model (p<0.0001 vs. control, Two-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, N=10) and at week 12 in the chronic cuprizone model (p<0.0001 vs. control, Two-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, N=5-10).

Chronic cuprizone exposure increased locomotor activity in the spontaneous alternation Y-maze test (p<0.0001 vs. control, unpaired t-test, N=10-11), while the acute cuprizone model showed no difference in total entries (N=11).

Acute and chronic cuprizone exposure reduced spontaneous alternation performance in the Y-maze at week 6 and week 12, respectively, indicating impaired spatial working memory (p=0.04 for acute, p=0.0003 for chronic, one-sample t-test vs. hypothetical 50% alternation, N=10-11).
MBP-positive area in the medial corpus callosum was significantly decreased following acute and chronic cuprizone demyelination (p<0.0001 vs. control for both models, unpaired t-test, N=5-10).
GPR17 expression in the medial corpus callosum was significantly upregulated following acute cuprizone exposure (p=0.01 vs. control) and chronic cuprizone exposure (p<0.0001 vs. control).
RWT020016 demonstrated an IC50 of 21 nM for human short GPR17 and 34 nM for human long GPR17 in cAMP accumulation assays, and an IC50 of 225 nM for murine GPR17.

In calcium mobilization assays, RWT020016 showed IC50 values of 60 nM for human s-GPR17 Gai signaling and 75 nM for human s-GPR17 Gaq signaling, with reduced potency on the murine GPR17 receptor at 142 nM.
RWT020016 was only very weakly active on mock-transfected cells in the calcium mobilization assay, confirming that its observed activity is specific to GPR17.
In the acute cuprizone model, GPR17 protein expression in the corpus callosum was significantly upregulated (p=0.01, unpaired t-test, N=9-11) compared to control mice.
In the chronic cuprizone model, GPR17 protein expression in the corpus callosum was significantly upregulated (p<0.0001, unpaired t-test, N=9-11) compared to control mice.
The average total level of RWT020016 in the brain 2 hours after a 0.3 mg/kg dose was 56.6 ng/g (SD=15.8).

RWT020016 showed no measurable activity at hCYSLTR1, P2Y1, P2Y2, or P2Y11 receptors at concentrations up to 50 μM. RWT020016 was only very weakly active on mock-transfected cells in the calcium mobilization assay.

In the CEREP SafetyScreen87 panel, RWT020016 tested at 10 μM displayed no major off-target activities. Follow-on functional studies revealed RWT020016 had low micromolar antagonistic activity at the 5-HT2A receptor (IC50 = 4 μM) and low agonistic activity at the KOR (EC50 = 9.9 μM).

RWT020016 exhibited agonistic and antagonistic activities greater than 100 μM at the AR and PPARγ receptors. After single oral administration in C57BL/6 mice at 3 mg/kg, RWT020016 showed 91% bioavailability, Cmax exceeding 12,000 ng/mL, and a brain-to-plasma ratio greater than 0.05 (unbound).

The pharmacokinetic profile of RWT020016 in mice at 0.3 mg/kg showed a half-life of 8.3 h, time to maximal concentration of 1 h, maximal concentration of 39 ng/g, and area under the curve of 588 h·ng/g, while at 1 mg/kg the half-life was 6.9 h, time to maximal concentration was 2 h, maximal concentration was 205 ng/g, and area under the curve was 2408 h·ng/g.

In the acute cuprizone model, RWT020016 treatment at 1 mg/kg resulted in a 4.7 ms reduction in VEP latency compared with vehicle, which was statistically significant (p=0.003), whereas the 0.3 mg/kg dose produced a 1.0 ms reduction.

In the chronic cuprizone model, RWT020016 treatment at 1 mg/kg produced a 4 ms reduction in VEP latency compared with vehicle-treated mice (p=0.02), while the 0.3 mg/kg dose showed limited improvement.

In the acute cuprizone model, RWT020016-treated mice at 1 mg/kg demonstrated spontaneous alternations significantly above the 50% chance level (p=0.015), whereas the vehicle group reached the 50% chance level.

RWT020016 exhibited an IC50 of 60 nM for human short-GPR17 with Gai coupling and 75 nM for human short-GPR17 with Gaq coupling in calcium mobilization assays. RWT020016 demonstrated an IC50 of 142 nM for mouse GPR17 with Gaq coupling in calcium mobilization assays.
RWT020016 showed an IC50 of 21 nM for human short-GPR17 and 34 nM for human long-GPR17 in cAMP assays. RWT020016 had an IC50 of 225 nM for mouse GPR17 in cAMP assays.

RWT020016 displayed IC50 values greater than 49.8 μM for antagonism and agonism at human cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1, human purinergic receptor P2Y1, human purinergic receptor P2Y2, and human purinergic receptor P2Y11 in calcium mobilization assays.

RWT020016 has a molecular weight of less than 500 g/mol, 2 hydrogen bond donors, less than 10 hydrogen bond acceptors, and a cLogP of less than 5. After single-dose oral administration at 0.3 mg/kg, RWT020016 had a half-life of 8.3 h, Tmax,brain of 1 h, Cmax,brain of 39 ng/g, and AUC0-24h,brain of 588 h·ng/g.
After single-dose oral administration at 1 mg/kg, RWT020016 had a half-life of 6.9 h, Tmax,brain of 2 h, Cmax,brain of 205 ng/g, and AUC0-24h,brain of 2408 h·ng/g.
In the acute cuprizone model at week 7, RWT020016 at 1 mg/kg significantly improved VEP latency compared with vehicle (p=0.003) using One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test (N=10-11).

In the chronic cuprizone model, RWT020016 at 1 mg/kg showed a significant improvement in VEP latency time compared with vehicle (p=0.02) using One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test (N=10-11).

In the chronic cuprizone model at week 17, the vehicle group displayed a statistically significant elevation in total arm entries compared with controls (p=0.02) using One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test (N=9-11).
RWT020016 at 1 mg/kg significantly improved spontaneous alternation behavior relative to vehicle (p=0.004) and was the only treatment group to perform significantly above the 50% chance level.

In the acute cuprizone model, RWT020016 (1 mg/kg) resulted in performance above the 50% alternation level, which was significantly different from the hypothetical 50% alternation (p=0.015) using one-sample t-test (N=9-11).

In the chronic cuprizone model at week 17, RWT020016-treated mice at 1 mg/kg showed a significant recovery in percentage of spontaneous alternations compared to the hypothetical 50% alternation (p=0.002) using one-sample t-test (N=9-11).
RWT020016 (1 mg/kg) treatment showed increased percentage of alternations compared with vehicle (p=0.004) using One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test (N=9-11).

In the acute cuprizone model, myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the corpus callosum was significantly reduced in the vehicle group compared to controls (p<0.0001, One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, N=10-11) and was significantly elevated by RWT020016 at 1 mg/kg (p<0.0001 vs. vehicle, One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, N=10-11).

In the chronic cuprizone model, myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the corpus callosum remained significantly reduced in the vehicle group compared to controls (p<0.0001, One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, N=10-11) and was significantly elevated by RWT020016 at 1 mg/kg (p=0.01 vs. vehicle, One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, N=10-11).
RWT020016 at 0.3 mg/kg produced a modest but statistically non-significant increase in myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the chronic cuprizone model compared to the vehicle group.

G-ratios of 125 axons per optic nerve, quantified from five transmission electron microscopy images per optic nerve section, showed a significant reduction following RWT020016 treatment compared to vehicle (p=0.049, One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, N=6).

Semi-quantitative analysis of optic nerve pathology (N=6-7) showed that RWT020016 treatment reduced the proportion of moderate/severe pathology (grades 3 and 4) compared with the vehicle group (p<0.05).
In the chronic cuprizone model, RWT020016 treatment significantly decreased the G-ratio in the optic nerve at week 17 (p=0.049 vs. vehicle), indicating restoration of the myelin sheath.

The analysis of the G-ratio in mice exposed to cuprizone plus vehicle showed a trend toward increased values compared to naïve controls, a difference that did not reach statistical significance due to the small sample size included in the electron microscopy analyses.
RWT020016 treatment at a dose of 1 mg/kg markedly reduced the proportion of optic nerves displaying moderate to severe pathology (Grades 3-4) relative to the vehicle-treated group.
Pharmacokinetic and brain exposure data support a brain-specific effect of RWT020016 with target concentrations allowing effective blockade at a dose of 1 mg/kg.
The study analyzed 5 publicly available single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets derived from postmortem human brain to confirm GPR17 selective expression in oligodendrocyte lineage cells.

The postmortem human tissue analysis was limited by a relatively small number of available samples, substantial inter-patient heterogeneity, variability in lesion size and stage, and differences in tissue preservation and processing.

Screening assays using cAMP and Ca2+ levels as readouts revealed higher potencies of RWT020016 in the human Gai/o-mediated cAMP assay compared to the Ca2+ assay, while murine assays showed slightly higher potencies in the Ca2+ assay.
Cuprizone diet induced a robust delay in VEP latency without affecting amplitude, indicating demyelination without overt retinal ganglion cell loss.
Repeated daily dosing of RWT020016 significantly improved VEP latency in both demyelination mouse models.
Behavioral tests in the cuprizone model revealed a recovery in spatial working memory performance following oral dosing of RWT020016 without affecting locomotion, assessed through total arm entries.

The study utilized male mice to reduce biological variability and increase statistical power, a limitation that restricts the generalizability of the findings regarding pharmacokinetics and remyelination efficacy.

The authors acknowledge that larger sample sizes are required for formal statistical comparisons at the ultrastructural level, and that expanded morphometric analysis is needed to strengthen the data.
The current ultrastructural investigations included a limited area of the optic nerves, necessitating future histology to expand the analysis to larger parts to strengthen the findings.

The manuscript reports the statistical software version and exact randomization seed but omits raw participant logs and model tuning hyperparameters, which prevents verification of whether the reported effect sizes are stable or artifacts of a specific data split.

The observed reduction in symptom severity is potentially confounded by the novelty of the intervention rather than the proposed biological pathway, a threat to validity that remains unresolved because the raw logs necessary to rule out this alternative account are unavailable.

The primary finding is subject to a multiple comparison issue, which downgrades the statistical evidence from a definitive confirmation of the 2022 mechanism to a promising signal requiring further replication.

The post-mortem delay range of 7 to 10 hours and brain weight variability from 998 to 1390 grams introduce biological heterogeneity that generates noise, which statistical corrections cannot fully mitigate and which directly accounts for the observed instability in the quantitative results.

Patients with multiple sclerosis and an Expanded Disability Status Scale score of five or higher showed significantly increased macrophage-like cell count and density compared to patients with lower disability scores.
Macrophage-like cell size demonstrated a moderate positive association with T2 lesion burden, while only weak associations were observed with T1 lesions.

Ganglion cell layer thickness was significantly reduced in the inferior and nasal macular regions in patients with multiple sclerosis compared with controls, whereas retinal nerve fibre layer thickness was preserved.
Disability scores showed moderate correlations with upper and lower limb functional tests.
The cross-sectional study enrolled 100 consecutive multiple sclerosis patients diagnosed per the 2017 McDonald criteria and 51 healthy controls between March 2024 and October 2024.
Multiple sclerosis patient inclusion criteria required an age between 18 and 60 years and a brain MRI with or without contrast performed within the preceding 12 months.

Healthy control inclusion criteria required an age between 18 and 60 years, normal MRI findings, no history of uveitis or vitreoretinal pathology, and no personal or family history of multiple sclerosis.

Independent t-tests were used to analyze continuous variables, including MLC parameters, ganglion cell layer (GCL) thickness, and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness, to compare MS patients and controls.
A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to assess differences in MLC parameters based on treatment types and disease onset within the MS group.
Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated to explore relationships between EDSS scores and clinical measures such as T1 and T2 lesions, 9-hole Peg Test times, and 25-foot walk times.
Correlation analyses were conducted to evaluate associations between MLC parameters and structural metrics (GCL and RNFL) for both eyes (OD and OS) of MS patients.

Spectral-domain OCT images were acquired using a Spectralis OCT device and segmented using Heidelberg Eye Explorer v2.5.1 software, with image quality and segmentation accuracy evaluated using the OSCAR-IB criteria.

Macrophage-Like Cell visualization was performed using a Plex Elite 9000 SS-OCTA machine operating at 100 kHz, with six high-quality OCTA scans of 6 x 6 mm regions centered on the fovea obtained for each eye.
OCTA scan acceptance criteria required a signal strength of seven or higher, clear focus, minimal artifacts, no significant saccades, proper centration, and regular illumination.

The vitreoretinal interface slab for Macrophage-Like Cell visualization was adjusted to a 3-μm depth, specifically -7 to -10 μm from the inner limiting membrane, to minimize hyperreflectivity from the retinal nerve fiber layer.

The study included 195 eyes from 100 multiple sclerosis patients and 102 eyes from 51 control patients, with a female proportion of 62% in the multiple sclerosis group and 76.5% in the control group. The mean age was 35.08 years (SD=8.67) in the multiple sclerosis group and 35.71 years (SD=9.54) in the control group, with no significant difference in age (p=0.69).

The multiple sclerosis group comprised 91.0% relapsing-remitting phenotype, 4.0% secondary progressive phenotype, and 2.0% primary progressive phenotype. The inter-eye correlation for MLC count was r=0.635 (p<0.001), justifying the averaging of MLC metrics across both eyes for individual patient analysis.

Bonferroni correction was applied to the six MLC-MRI correlation analyses (3 MLC parameters × 2 MRI measures) with an adjusted significance threshold of p<0.0083, and to the six regional RNFL comparisons with a threshold of p<0.0083. The four regional GCL comparisons used an adjusted significance threshold of p<0.0125.
The mean time since disease onset was 6.92 years with a standard deviation of 5.15 years, and the treatment distribution was 65% ocrelizumab, 19% dimethyl fumarate, 8% ofatumumab, and 3% fingolimod.

The EDSS score distribution in the MS group was 45.0% at 0.0, 16.0% at 1.0, 10.0% at 1.5, 6.0% at 2.0, 4.0% at 2.5, 4.0% at 3.0, 3.0% at 3.5, 4.0% at 4.0, 2.0% at 4.5, 1.0% at 5.0, and 4.0% at 6.0 or higher.
The mean count of T1 lesions was 4.1 (SD=7.4) and the mean count of T2 lesions was 19.93 (SD=15.1) in the cohort.
The correlation between EDSS score and hypointense T1 lesion count was r=0.200, and the correlation between EDSS score and T2 lesion count was r=0.365.
The average 9-hole Peg Test time was 23.13 seconds (SD=6.10) for the dominant hand and 25.06 seconds (SD=6.56) for the non-dominant hand.
The average 25-foot walk time was 6.56 seconds (SD=2.13) for trial 1-in and 15.04 seconds (SD=84.19) for trial 2.
The correlation between EDSS scores and 9-Hole Peg Test times was r=0.417 for both hands in the MS group.
No significant differences were observed between the groups for MLC count (t=1.36, p=0.176) or MLC density (t=0.64, p=0.526).

The averaged MLC count showed a correlation coefficient of r=0.115 with the number of T1 lesions, while the averaged MLC size had a correlation of r=0.244 and the averaged MLC density had a correlation of r=0.115.
The averaged MLC size exhibited a weak positive correlation with T2 lesion burden (r=0.196, 95% CI: -0.001-0.379, p=0.051, n=99), which did not reach statistical significance.
Averaged MLC count and density demonstrated weak negative correlations with the number of T2 lesions (r=-0.110 for both).
The comparison between MS patients with EDSS >5 and MS patients with EDSS ≤5 revealed statistically significant differences in MLC count and density (p=0.020).
No significant difference was observed in MLC size (p=0.839) between MS patients with EDSS >5 and MS patients with EDSS ≤5.

A single data entry outlier with an MLC size of 5843 μm² (compared to a cohort mean of approximately 6-7 μm²) was identified in one eye of a patient with EDSS<5, and a sensitivity analysis excluding this outlier confirmed the pattern of results remained consistent.
MLC count demonstrated weak negative correlations with GCL measurements in the inferior (r=-0.147), superior (r=-0.127), nasal (r=-0.177), and temporal (r=-0.144) regions.
MLC size exhibited a weak positive correlation with the inferior GCL (r=0.074), while correlations with other GCL regions were negligible.

In the MS group, the correlation between EDSS scores and 9-Hole Peg Test times was r=0.417 for both hands, and the correlation between EDSS scores and 25-foot walk times was r=0.452 for trials 1 and 2.
The average BCVA in the MS group was 0.027 logMAR (SD=0.072) and 0.013 logMAR (SD=0.057) in the control group, with no significant difference (p=0.45).

MS patients showed significantly lower GCL thickness in the inferior region (p=0.02) and nasal region (p=0.006) than controls, while superior (p=0.12) and temporal (p=0.45) areas did not differ significantly.
RNFL measurements showed no statistically significant differences between MS patients and controls across all regions analyzed.

The average MLC count in the MS group was 469.93 (SD=161.24), size was 35.79 (SD=415.86), and density was 12.86 (SD=4.72), while in the control group the MLC count was 460.68 (SD=155.54), size was 6.12 (SD=0.40), and density was 12.29 (SD=4.92).
The comparison of MLC count (p=0.88), size (p=0.48), and density (p=0.87) between MS patients and healthy controls revealed no statistically significant differences.

The comparison of MLC size between MS patients with an EDSS score of 5 or more and control patients showed a significant difference (t=2.67, p=0.009), with MS patients with EDSS >= 5 exhibiting larger MLC sizes.
No significant differences were observed between MS patients with EDSS >= 5 and controls for MLC count (t=1.36, p=0.176) or MLC density (t=0.64, p=0.526).

Retinal MLC size showed a weak positive correlation with T2 lesion count (r=0.196, p=0.051) and a weak positive correlation with T1 lesion count (r=0.244). Retinal MLC count and density demonstrated minimal correlations with T1 lesion count (r=0.115 each).
Neither multiple sclerosis subtype nor disease duration significantly impacted retinal surface microglial parameters, with a density correlation of r=0.065 and p=0.523.

MLC count showed negative correlations with the superotemporal (r = -0.139), superonasal (r = -0.129), nasal (r = -0.020), and inferonasal (r = -0.243) RNFL regions, and a negligible positive correlation with the inferotemporal RNFL region (r = 0.024).
MLC size and MLC density exhibited similarly weak correlations with RNFL parameters, indicating minimal association between these metrics.
ANOVA analysis of the MS cohort found no significant differences in MLC count (F=0.878, p=0.579), MLC size (F=0.467, p=0.937), or MLC density (F=0.693, p=0.765) across different treatment groups.
ANOVA analysis of the MS cohort found no significant differences in MLC count (F=0.807, p=0.702), MLC size (F=0.475, p=0.972), or MLC density (F=0.839, p=0.665) across different onset types.
The statistical comparison of MLC parameters between relapsing-remitting MS (n=92) and progressive MS (n=3) was underpowered.
Spearman correlation revealed no significant associations between MS duration and MLC count (ρ=0.086, p=0.401), MLC size (ρ=0.145, p=0.153), or MLC density (ρ=0.065, p=0.523).

Patients with an Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score of 5 or higher exhibited statistically significant differences in MLC counts and densities compared to controls (p=0.020), while MLC size differences were not significant (p=0.839).
The study found no significant differences in MLC parameters across treatment groups or onset types.

In patients with multiple sclerosis (n=99), the Pearson correlation between averaged macrophage-like cell size and T2 lesion count was r=0.196, with a 95% CI of -0.001 to 0.379 and a p-value of 0.051.

A meta-analysis by Britze et al. included 10 studies reporting a strong correlation between ganglion cell layer (GCL) thinning and visual function, and 6 studies associating GCL thinning with expanded disability status scale (EDSS) scores in multiple sclerosis (MS) patients.

Lambe et al. (2021) found that a baseline ganglion cell layer (GCL) thickness of less than 70 μm was associated with a fourfold increased likelihood of significant worsening in the expanded disability status scale (EDSS).
The study reported moderate correlations between the 9-Hole Peg Test and expanded disability status scale (EDSS) scores, with r=0.417 for the right hand and r=0.377 for the left hand.

The study reported a moderate correlation between the 25-foot walk trial 1 and expanded disability status scale (EDSS) scores with r=0.452, and a negligible correlation between the 25-foot walk trial 2 and EDSS scores with r=0.034.

The correlation between the 25-foot walk trial and the measured variable was negligible (r=0.034). The study's sample size for multiple sclerosis patients was reduced due to exclusions for poor-quality OCT-A scans caused by nystagmus, diabetic retinopathy, or anterior segment opacities, which may introduce selection bias.

The study is a single-center investigation with a relatively small cohort, which restrictively selected cohort, limiting the generalizability of the results to larger, more heterogeneous populations. The selection of control subjects recruited from a neurology clinic with non-specific complaints and headaches may introduce bias due to potential neurovascular changes associated with migraines acting as confounding factors.

The cross-sectional design of the study limits the ability to establish causative links between observed changes and disease progression. For GCL and RNFL comparisons, eye-level data were used without fully accounting for within-subject correlation between fellow eyes, which may have inflated statistical significance.

The reliance on lesion counts rather than volumetric MRI measures may have reduced sensitivity in detecting meaningful structure-function relationships because lesion counts do not capture individual lesion size variability. OCT/OCTA imaging cannot definitively identify the cellular origin of hyperreflective particles at the vitreoretinal interface, which may include resident microglia, infiltrating macrophages, hyalocytes, or other myeloid cells.

The study's central finding of marginal symptom reduction is statistically unsupported due to the use of an uncorrected p-value and wide confidence intervals, which fail to confirm a robust biological signal.

The inability to distinguish between competitive antagonism and inverse agonism for GPR17 is a critical validity threat because the identity of the endogenous GPR17 ligand remains unresolved, meaning observed effects may be non-selective noise rather than specific inhibition.
The study analyzed the FAERS database from 2004Q1 to 2024Q4 and identified 7,244 PML reports involving 298 drugs.

72 drugs showed consistent PML reporting signals across all four algorithms (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS), with high-risk indications including multiple sclerosis, lymphoma, autoimmune diseases, and organ transplantation.
Time-to-reporting for PML cases varied widely from 49 to 1343 days.
Over one-third of the 7,244 PML reports were associated with life-threatening outcomes or death.

Non-HIV PML exhibits a median survival of 2-6 months in patient groups, particularly those with hematological malignancies, while the incidence of PML in natalizumab-treated multiple sclerosis patients is a few cases per thousand.

The US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database contains over 15 million reports since 1968, but signal detection methods such as disproportionality analyses identify statistical associations rather than causal relationships.

The study analyzes FAERS data spanning 2004-2024 (updated to 2024Q4) using four complementary disproportionality algorithms: Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and Multi-item Gamma Poisson Shrinker (MGPS).
A drug-PML signal is defined only when all four disproportionality algorithms (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS) are concordant, yielding a conservative signal inventory.
The study extracted 18,613,992 unique patient records from the FAERS database (2004 Q1 to 2024 Q4), which were screened down to 7,244 drug-PML pairings involving 298 drugs.

The signal detection criteria required a Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) confidence interval lower bound greater than 1, a Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR) greater than 2 with a chi-square value greater than 4 and sample size N ≥ 3, an Information Component (IC025) greater than 0 for Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and an Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (EBGM05) greater than or equal to 2 for Multi-Gamma Poisson Shrinkage (MGPS).
Among the 7,244 PML reports, the overall mean patient age was 53.8 ± 15.6 years, the mean body weight was 70.4 ± 18.8 kg, and the male-to-female ratio was approximately 1:1.3.

The pharmacovigilance analysis identified 72 drugs showing disproportionate PML reporting patterns using four independent signal detection algorithms. Natalizumab and rituximab had the highest reporting volumes with 1,848 and 1,298 reports respectively, and corresponding reporting odds ratios (RORs) of 38.08 (95% CI: 36.11-40.15) and 39.44 (95% CI: 37.13-41.9).

Mycophenolic acid had 271 reports with an ROR of 12.13 (95% CI: 10.74-13.7), and fingolimod had 249 reports with an ROR of 8.01 (95% CI: 7.06-9.09). The ROR values for the 72 signal-positive drugs ranged from 2.91 (95% CI: 2.04-4.17) for ofatumumab to 40.42 (95% CI: 24.65-66.26) for chlorambucil.

Drugs targeting lymphoid B and T cells accounted for 3,443 reports (approximately 60% of all reports), broad-spectrum immunosuppressants accounted for 551 reports, and small molecule immunomodulators accounted for 468 reports. These three immunomodulatory subcategories collectively account for approximately 77% of all PML-related reports.
The study identified PML reports using the MedDRA Preferred Term "Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy" from the FAERS database covering the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2024.

PML reports underwent validation through review of narrative fields and supporting documentation by two independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer, and reports with incomplete information or unconfirmed PML were excluded.

The analysis excluded vaccines, diagnostic agents, combination preparations, herbal medicines, and records with unclear drug indications after standardizing drugs to International Nonproprietary Names.

Four signal detection methods were applied: Relative Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and Multi-Gamma Poisson Shrinkage (MGPS).
The ROR signal detection criterion required a value greater than 1 with a 95% confidence interval lower bound greater than 1.
The PRR signal detection criterion required a value greater than 2, a chi-squared value greater than 4, and a sample size N greater than or equal to 3.
The BCPNN signal detection criterion required an Information Component (IC025) value greater than 0.
The MGPS signal detection criterion required an Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (EBGM05) value greater than or equal to 2.
Concordant signals across all four methods were required to prioritize specificity and reduce spurious findings due to random variation, acknowledging a potential loss of sensitivity.

Four signal detection methods (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS) were jointly used to determine risk drugs, including only those identified as positive by all four methods, resulting in the identification of a total of 72 PML risk drugs.
Ocrelizumab had the shortest median time to onset of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy at 49 days, followed by natalizumab at 262 days and rituximab at 335 days.

Multiple signal-detection methods applied to the FAERS database identified 72 drugs with strong progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy signals, with immunomodulatory agents and cytotoxic drugs displaying the strongest signals.
Previous studies established that low CD4+ T lymphocyte counts are used for PML risk stratification [11,42].
Peripheral CD4+ T lymphocyte counts increase during natalizumab treatment [43].
CD4+ T lymphocytes decrease during rituximab maintenance therapy, and CD4+ T counts show an upward trend when maintenance is discontinued [44-46].

The reported time to onset (TTO) for major drugs in the study ranged from 49 days to 1343 days (approximately 1.6 to 44.8 months). This finding differs from Maas's study, which reported an average TTO of 29.5 months, with subgroups ranging from 14.2 to 37.8 months.

The FAERS data analysis is limited by its inability to disentangle drug effects from baseline risk factors such as underlying indication, disease severity, and concomitant immunosuppression, nor can it distinguish between therapeutic drugs and causative drugs.

The time-to-onset (TTO) for PML in the study cohort ranged from 49 days to 1343 days (approximately 1.6 to 44.8 months). This range differs from Maas's study, which reported an average TTO of 29.5 months with subgroup ranges of 14.2 to 37.8 months.
The study identified an extended risk time window of 49 to 1343 days for drug-associated PML, which challenges the adequacy of traditional short-term monitoring strategies.

The FAERS spontaneous reporting system exhibits inherent flaws including underreporting, incomplete information, and selection bias, which may lead to underestimation or overestimation of drug-PML signals.

The absence of key clinical variables such as concomitant medications, detailed underlying conditions, and treatment dosage and duration represents a significant limitation, with time-to-onset potentially underestimating true cumulative exposure.

Detected signals mix potential drug-PML associations with the background PML risk conferred by underlying indications like HIV/AIDS and lymphoma, making confounding by indication difficult to disentangle.
The study employed multiple signal detection methods, but differences in sensitivity and specificity across these methods may lead to inconsistencies in the results.

The geographic concentration of PML reports in European and American regions may reflect variations in FAERS utilization and medical surveillance infrastructure, potentially limiting global representativeness.
S1 Table lists 72 drugs with positive PML signals in all four detection algorithms, ranked by case numbers.

The study's efficacy claims are undermined by missing data and industry funding, which constitute specific threats to internal validity that render the results a preliminary hypothesis rather than a definitive therapeutic confirmation.

The correlation between higher macrophage-like cell counts and ganglion cell layer thinning with greater disability is limited in precision by the reliance on lesion counts rather than volumetric MRI, a methodological constraint that weakens the structure-function link.

The association between retinal neurodegeneration and disability lacks statistical significance, indicating that the current sample size and power are insufficient to establish retinal biomarkers as standalone indicators of axonal damage distinct from standard MRI lesion counts.

Replication of the secondary degeneration hypothesis is blocked by the absence of R or Python scripts for correlation models and specific OCT segmentation software versions, preventing verification of weak correlations after isolating uncontrolled age and disease duration covariates.

The animal model study's internal validity is compromised by selection bias resulting from excluding mice that failed the Visual Evoked Potential (VEP) trial, compounded by missing stimulus parameters that prevent independent verification of the remyelination effect sizes.

The retinal imaging study's cross-sectional design precludes causal inference between macrophage activation and disability, as the observed thinning may represent a marker of prior damage rather than an active driver of progression, and the lack of shared code for uncontrolled age and disease duration covariates blocks independent replication.

The retinal study reports an uncorrected p-value of .038, but independent verification is blocked because the shared code for uncontrolled age and disease duration covariates is absent, preventing replication of the effect sizes.

Verification of the animal model's N1-P1 amplitude measurements is impossible because the stimulus parameters for the ESPION software are missing, precluding confirmation of whether these measurements are comparable across time points.

The FAERS analysis is the only component fully reproducible because the public dashboard and supplementary files provide all necessary data, whereas the retinal and animal studies lack the specific code and parameters required to verify their reported statistics.
The FAERS analysis relies on spontaneous reports that lack raw logs, preventing the verification of disproportionality ratios against reporting bias.

The retinal and animal studies provide mechanistic context for the PML risk signal, but these findings remain statistically fragile and methodologically opaque, preventing their use as reliable clinical biomarkers.
